Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

Sherwood Waldron

Sherwood Waldron

Sherwood Waldron  

DISCUSSION: Dr. Andrew Peto referred to Imre Hermann's conceptualization of clinging versus going-in-search as a contrasting instinctual pair. He also examined the relevance of Willi Hoffer's description of hand-mouth coordination and its relation to the earliest forms of ego integration. Dr. Peto then mentioned his own ideas about transient interruption of part-self and part-object representations and their relation to depressive tendencies, and feelings of depersonalization. Dr. Manuel Furer cast Dr. Friedman's contribution in the historical perspective of a gradual change of analytic emphasis from recovery of the past via remembering to its recovery from reliving or repeating in the transference instead of remembering, especially in regard to preverbal experiences which would not be recoverable directly in memory (Greenacre). He felt that Dr. Friedman placed emphasis on a reconstructed memory from preverbal times, which Dr. Friedman felt was uncontaminated with contributions from later developmental epochs. On the basis of our understanding of the multiple determination of symptoms, Dr. Furer felt that such lack of contamination is not likely. He discussed the potential advantages and disadvantages of such reconstructions, and was not fully satisfied that this particular reconstruction was required, given the case material presented. He provided two of his own case illustrations of the symptom of dizziness. The first revealed the defensive development of this symptom to express the patient's unconscious guilt at comparing herself favorably with her aged, infirm mother, as well as her fear of talion reprisal. The other case appeared to reflect a blend of displaced orgiastic fantasies with rage at an unsupportive and unnurturing mother. He felt that the explanation offered by Dr. Friedman could lead an analyst to neglect the determining unconscious instinctual fantasies of a patient and the conflicts arising therefrom. At the same time, he felt that the ideas offered by Dr. Friedman helped to widen our consciousness of particular childhood experiences which can be useful to us in reconstructive work.

responseSet.title: Disorders of the Schizophrenic Syndrome: Edited by Leopold Bellak.  New York:  Basic Books, 1979.  629 pp.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Disorders of the Schizophrenic Syndrome

Edited by Leopold Bellak. New York: Basic Books, 1979. 629 pp.

Martin Blum

Martin Blum

Martin H. Blum
NEW YORK

Martin Blum  

In 1948 Leopold Bellak published a review of the prior decade's literature on schizophrenia. He has repeated the feat decennially, the present volume being the fourth in the series. This latest overview contains seventeen chapters, by twenty-three authors, devoted to such topics as the epidemiology, biochemistry, genetics, psychology, familial aspects, diagnosis, somatic treatment, psychotherapy, and prognosis of schizophrenia. Among them, these chapters contain 2,875 references to the literature, primarily of the last ten years. Each chapter represents a compact statement of our current understanding in a particular domain and also estimates and evaluates current trends in that domain.

The major events of the last decade in this field have been the increased documentation of the role of genetic factors and the growing doubts with regard to the dopamine hypothesis in its present form. The genetic studies are well reviewed by Robert Cancro, who includes a particularly sophisticated subessay on the theory of diagnosis. Cancro concludes that "the genetic studies do not rule out social interventions … the knowledge of the value of psychotherapy for certain patients derives from experience and cannot be refuted by a theoretical notion" (p. 149).

This defensive note with regard to dynamic treatment is, of course, a reference to the bias, which grew rapidly in American psychiatry of the sixties and seventies, that psychotherapy in any form is ineffective in the treatment of schizophrenia and therefore could not rationally be included in a treatment program. John Gunderson, in his chapter on psychotherapy, examines the evidence for this pessimism and finds it wanting. Nonetheless, he notes that "the psychotherapy of schizophrenia is at an impasse"; the acceptance of psychotherapy as a useful modality "which grew modestly but consistently from 1930 to 1960" has not continued to expand.

The entire volume, under Bellak's aegis, maintains an attitude consistent with Freud's commitment to the concept of a complementary series (between genetics and environment) in pathogenesis.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XL, 1976

Introductory Reflections on the Study of Some Active Factors in the Countertransference. Denise Braunschweig and Michel Fain. Pp. 483-540.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

In a previous article Braunschweig made the claim that the analyst is able to understand his patient by means of a hysterical identification with the patient. There has, however, been little discussion of this claim, possibly because it upsets the usual concepts on the dynamics of countertransference. Here the authors present the interesting thesis that there is a critical element which comes into play at the moment of hysterical identification. This critical aspect is an important organizing factor in the countertransference and helps balance out the resexualization involved as the analyst deviates from a neutral ideal toward an empathic understanding of the patient through hysterical identification. In his significant study of transference, Michel Neyraut stressed the importance of the countertransference in the acquisition of theoretical psychoanalytic knowledge. Braunschweig and Fain feel that this way of viewing the problem will end in a criticism of hysterical identification that will minimize its force and importance. In their tightly argued, polemical article they defend their emphasis on hysterical identification and attempt to show that countertransference can be explained metapsychologically by reference to their "critical element.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Parat discusses the factors involved in the choice of analysis as a profession, in the choice of a particular patient, and in the capacity to work with that patient. Countertransference is a privileged means of pursuing self-analysis. Although countertransference responses can contaminate or cause difficulty for analytic work, the countertransference-transference currents constitute part of the basic relationship between analyst and patient. Parat also discusses the various background problems in countertransference, the social and ethical frameworks, and the analyst as a witness to reality. Analytic work is inevitably lonely; there are narcissistic rewards as well as the dangers of disillusionment and disbelief in the possibility of real feelings.

Countertransference and Despair. Olivier Flournoy. Pp. 561-573.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Flournoy would reserve the term "countertransference" for those sudden and temporary regressions of the analyst which are motivated by a sentiment of despair in understanding the transference of the patient through the analytic method. The analyst's task is to turn the regression around—toward a new understanding or reconstruction of the transference. Only when the regression becomes lasting and disengagement impossible should we speak of a countertransference neurosis. Hence the countertransference has an operational value for assessing the conduct of treatment. Eventually, by the increasing rarity of its occurrence, it becomes of value in determining the time of termination.

299

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

As an experimental cognitive psychologist who has long been interested in problems raised by such American theorists as Chomsky, Lenneberg, Fodor,

299

Bever, and others, Mehler presents an overview of the development of academic psychology and draws certain parallels in psychoanalytic thinking. He cites the extensive research carried out by his group at the Centre National des Recherches Scientifiques in Paris concerning learning and memory in the newborn and in very young children. His findings have been important in indicating the linguistic sensitivity of the newborn and young children. He has delineated a shift from global to analytic memory, a shift which, he feels, must be linked to the acquisition of linguistic activity. He draws some conclusions concerning childhood amnesia and the use of different coding schemata before and after the period between the ages of three and six. He hopes for a closer interdisciplinary collaboration between psychoanalysis and contemporary cognitive psychology to further such research on language.

Freud often spoke of bridge-words (Wortbrücke), and Brousselle wishes to expand on one aspect of these word-bridges frequently encountered in treatment. Sometimes a word has two opposite meanings and permits both the representation of things and word representations. The author supplies some clinical examples and suggests that these word-bridges are often found in problems concerning denial.

Youth and Religious Cults: A Societal and Clinical Dilemma. Saul V. Levine. Pp. 75-89.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

Through extensive interviews with one hundred six young (median age twenty-one and a half years) members of nine religious "fringe groups," the author attempts to clarify the psychological reasons for joining such cults as well as the effect on young people of being members. He finds that these people were all unhappy and alienated before joining, though he finds little evidence of serious psychopathology. It seems that many group members benefited from conversion in the sense that they felt much better, although the author finds a "closed-mindedness" among them. He concludes that, rather than simply "joining the chorus of diatribe" against religious cults, we should instead encourage alternatives for youth in our society.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

In a thoughtful, straightforward paper, rich in detailed case studies, the authors describe a survey of one thousand one hundred ninety-five university students (1971-1973). An attempt is made to understand the psychological makeup of politically radical students in a fashion more objective than that of the highly conflicting analyses appearing in the literature of the late 1960's and the early 1970's. Compared with "liberal" and "conservative" students,

141

the radicals "scored high on the need for power, low on the need for affiliation, low on impulse control, high on defensive projection." Nearly forty volunteers were given psychological tests and interviewed in depth. Several of these cases are described. The authors, unlike others who have perceived student radicals as a "new breed," find that the interviewees were experiencing classical, recognizable adolescent crises; they can be understood in psychoanalytic terms. We should question our own unconscious motivations if we find any political and social judgments intruding upon our clinical observations.

142

The authors, already long involved in the study of the psychology of the victims of the Holocaust and of their children, conducted an attitude survey among two hundred eleven Israeli children and ninety-seven Jewish-American children, all aged thirteen to fourteen. Some children in each sample were children of Holocaust survivors. The children were asked to express their feelings about Germans in general and about a hypothetical German agemate. The most striking finding in this study was the difference in response between the Israeli children of Holocaust survivors and their American counterparts. The Israeli children (living in a country where feelings about the Holocaust are openly and frequently expressed) responded with direct expressions of hostility. The American children showed massive denial of feelings. The authors postulate that these latter children are continuing the suppression of aggression so commonly found in their parents, the survivors, which has been associated with frequent depressive states.

142

Adolescent Turmoil: A Myth Revisited. David G. Oldham. Pp. 267-279.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

Once again, the concept that serious turmoil is the norm in adolescent development is reviewed and challenged. Oldham reviews briefly and succinctly: 1) the literature (e.g., Anna Freud, Spiegel, Fountain, Josselyn) suggesting that disruption of psychic equilibrium resulting in overt signs of turmoil is normal in adolescence; 2) the literature (e.g., Dovan and Adelson, Offer, Masterson) surveying nonpatient adolescent groups, suggesting that adolescents normally maintain psychic equilibrium with only mild and transient anxiety, depression, and minor disagreements with family; and 3) those factors in our profession and in society which serve to maintain what he terms "the myth" of the normality of severe adolescent turmoil, in the face of much evidence to the contrary.

The Art Work as a Force in the Artist's Life: Thomas Mann's Exile and "Joseph and His Brothers." George C. Rosenwald. Pp. 519-562.

Michael Trupp

Michael Trupp

Michael Trupp  

This expert polemic on the nature of psychological momentum in creativity uses Mann's lifelong experience of "emotional" and, later, actual exile. The discussion combines considerations of objectivist theory and aesthetics, suggesting that neither private dynamics (including the expressive or adaptational vicissitudes

thereof) nor cultural and historic influence can explain major artistic production. Artistic force, according to this view, both shapes and is shaped by all of these. The reading of the Eissler and Rosenwald papers back-to-back is recommended.

Self-Control and Self-Assurance: New Techniques of Behavior Therapy. Hans-Geert Metzger. Pp. 29-62.

Changing syndromes and corresponding new therapeutic requirements have forced theorists of behavior therapy to extend their domain of intervention, including innovations concerning self and self-esteem conflict and the tacit relinquishment of certain "classical" principles. The innovations are consistent with the general program of behavior therapy: disturbances are isolated and removed by training. To ignore the life-historical meaning context of symptoms is to promote the unwitting adaptation of individuals to the prevailing forms of interaction.

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. VI, 1978

Psychoanalysis and Biography. Joseph Lichtenberg. Pp. 397-427.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The author compares biographical sketches from different epochs, as well as biographies and autobiographies of famous persons, such as St. Augustine, Benvenuto Cellini, Samuel Johnson, and Eugene O'Neill. He shows how, even before Freud, early biographers used many "Freudian" insights, albeit in a disorganized fashion. With the advent of psychoanalysis, biographies are seen to be greatly enriched by psychoanalytic insights and experience. The author states, "Though I believe the paths of biography and psychoanalysis intersect, they do not and should not converge. The great biographers of the past created their masterworks from a unity of knowledge which they then shared with the reader." One must recognize that psychoanalysis considers not only the psychoanalytic importance of the biography itself, but also the psychoanalytic insights of the biographer. Thus different biographers will select different emphases for the development of their themes.

455

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. VI, 1978

A Hypothesis Regarding the Origins of Freud's Concepts of the Psychology of Adolescence. George H. Klumpner. Pp. 3-22.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The author uses Freud's 1905 work, Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality, as the basis of his observations. He indicates that Freud's conclusions about adolescence were derived more from anecdotal and historical material than from actual subjects. Although he states that Freud was concerned primarily with the third of the essays, "The Transformations of Puberty," later in his article Klumpner maintains that the key to the origin of Freud's ideas about adolescence can be found in the second essay. Freud usually used the inductive method to arrive at his conclusions, but in regard to adolescence he used the deductive method. Klumpner supports his thesis by systematically showing how Freud's theories of adolescence did not arise from: 1) observations of his own children; 2) his self-analysis; or 3) his clinical work with adolescents.

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. VI, 1978

Oedipus and America: Historical Perspectives on the Reception of Psychoanalysis in the United States. John Demos. Pp. 23-39.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

Demos begins with a comment attributed to Freud by Jones, to the effect that America was a mistake. By this Freud meant that the nature of the acceptance of psychoanalysis in America was a mistake. The main thrust of this article is to show how various cultural and psychological factors laid the foundation for the eagerness with which psychoanalysis was received in America. Demos cites such phenomena as the cult of motherhood, a shift in attitudes toward child rearing based more on guilt than on shame, the declining birthrate, the sense of the exclusive responsibility among family members for one another, and the kind of oedipal rivalry between father and son that includes the expectation that the son will outdo his rival. Perhaps the most interesting of all the fascinating references in this article is one in which a Congregational minister is quoted as having said, "Let every Christian father and mother understand that when the child is three years old, they have done more than half of what they will do for his character." Such a quotation epitomizes the richness of the ambience for the success of psychoanalysis in America. On the other hand, the author does not overlook the tremendous resistances to the psychoanalytic movement.

450

The Annual of Psychoanalysis. VI, 1978

A Grammar for the Humanities. John E. Gedo. Pp. 75-102.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

Gedo covers a rather large area in an attempt to show that psychoanalysis has much to offer the humanities. He uses five areas in which to prove his points: 1) biographical studies of one life; 2) fictional characters, in whom a richness of traits is often focused in one individual; 3) aesthetics and creativity (perhaps the most difficult part of this article because of the multiplicity of factors involved); 4) psychohistory, an area to which he feels that Waelder has probably made the most substantial contribution; and 5) moral philosophy. Among the reasons that psychoanalysis has made great contributions to the humanities are: its love of truth and rationality, its demands for detachment, disinterestedness, and hard work, its curiosity, and its dedication to humility. Gedo concludes that "it is by means of these ideals above all that psychoanalysis has reintroduced the humanist outlook into the realm of science." His thesis is well documented through the sensitivity with which he studies the outlined areas.

451

The Transference Enactment of Early Body-Image Determinants. J. Gordon Maguire. Pp. 181-207.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

Despite the title's apparent relevance to the content of this article, the case presentation is more an example of Kohut's notion that, in many analyses, oedipal and preoedipal conflicts are analyzed, while the narcissistic components of character structure are left unanalyzed. In this instance, the patient had had a previous analysis in which the oedipal and preoedipal object relationships and conflicts had been analyzed, but the basic narcissistic core had been left

452

untouched, leading to a failure in the analysis. The author does justice to the patient's first analysis but shows how it was incomplete by virtue of the neglect of narcissistic features. Nevertheless, it is difficult to evaluate the degree of responsiveness of the patient to this theoretical concept; it is equally conceivable that the results of the second analysis were based on his being allowed to develop in the ambience of an extremely patient and empathic observer.

Meeting of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

October 30, 1979. TWO PHOBIC VARIANTS. M. Donald Coleman, M.D.

Dr. Coleman focused on two distinct syndromes which he believes to be phobic variants: "developmental phobias" and "mid-life phobias." He described the developmental phobia as a type of agoraphobia which appears traceable to the separation-individuation phase. Conflicts that arise from the oedipal period, "while evident, do not appear to be decisive in determining pathology… Those cases I am most familiar with clinically seem to have resulted almost entirely from maternal pathology." The mother in such cases has manifested marked hostility toward the child's developing autonomy, and the child has had to deal internally with hostility toward the mother. Since such a mother finds manifestations of hostility from the child to be intolerable indications of autonomy, so eventually will the child. In therapy in adulthood, these patients' "line of development, i.e., the need for symbiosis to respond to the mother's needs, should be seen as a logical, adaptive mode of a child in dealing with the perceived mother." Special tact is necessary if the analyst needs to demonstrate that the patient's current love object has attitudes toward autonomy similar to the mother's. Drawing on his clinical experience with a patient, Dr. Coleman stated that the analyst's lack of tact in relation to this type of current love object may be the rock on which therapy founders. He described a patient's therapy which has been conducted twice weekly for the past four years and has resulted in marked relief of her agoraphobia. Extensive reconstruction of the reality of her relationship with her mother and her adaptive responses to that reality had been of considerable value. Conflicts over oedipal impulses had emerged but at that time "did not appear to have been decisive in the formation of the patient's pathology, although it is clear that conflicts of sexuality and castration anxiety caused the last increment of anxiety that made her seek out therapy." Dr. Coleman believes that a modified technique may be required for cases in which there is a primacy of separation-individuation problems in the genesis of the phobic-like illness. He stated, "An analytic approach which emphasizes the silent, unseen analyst or which focuses on early cues of the patient's fear of her sexual and aggressive impulses would seem destined to failure." He suggested early emphasis on reconstruction of the "real" nature of the mother-child dyad and its phase-related perceptual distortions. In commenting on Weinstock's 1959 study in which only six of forty-six completely analyzed phobic patients became symptom-free, Dr. Coleman suggested that the group may have included many patients with genetics and dynamics similar to his patients' "developmental phobias"; hence the relative refractoriness of the phobias to analyses which may assume a higher level of structural conflict.

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

November 19, 1979. THE CURRENT PSYCHOANALYTIC DIALOGUE: ITS COUNTERPART IN RENAISSANCE PHILOSOPHY. Simon A. Grolnick, M.D.

Dr. Grolnick discussed an important area of concern to psychoanalysts today: the debate between the "classical" or "structural" theorists and their critics. The critics (Kohut, Winnicott, Schafer, and Loewald were mentioned in this paper) reactively respond to certain theoretical, technical, philosophical, and methodological premises of classical psychoanalysis. Among the cogent philosophical problems are those which involve these pairs: determinism and freedom, subject and object, natural science and human or cultural science, logic and emotion, and art and science. Dr. Grolnick believes it is pertinent that these same dualities existed as vital questions during the Renaissance. The dialectical solutions that emerged at that time were fostered in part by the continuing interplay of Neo-Platonist thought and Aristotelian influences.

Arthur Lew

Arthur Lew

Arthur Lew  

DISCUSSION: Dr. Joseph T. Coltrera questioned Dr. Grolnick's confidence in a progressive dialectic leading to a new synthesis of psychoanalytic theories. He also questioned Dr. Grolnick's view of the Renaissance as a historical parallel, citing political factors as outweighing any rational dialectic in determining the historically ascendant point of view. Dr. Coltrera directed attention instead to the nineteenth century "and its central philosophical concerns for language and meaning." He outlined the development of the notion of "mind as an enduring psychic structure whose categorical imperative is to impose meaning on its experience of a unique self and its object world." He pointed out the methodological problem entailed in the concept of the self as both structure and process. A similar "conceptual embarrassment" was resolved by Freud in his "metapsychological papers": Freud proposed the drive-wish as the cognate form of the instinctual drive. Thereafter, drive-wishes became validly interpretable on the conceptual order of meaning rather than on the disparate order of force, a valid connection thus having been made "within the unconscious" between an instinctual drive and an idea. This metapsychological formulation has been continued in modern ego psychology's emphasis on the synthetic functions of the ego and has direct implications for modern notions of interpretation and reconstruction. Dr. Coltrera concluded that a clear theoretical view of narcissism and of the self was not achieved by Freud largely because of his overriding concern with the necessity of first clarifying the concept of psychic structure. Thus, the distinction between self and ego had to await the contributions of Hartmann and Jacobson. The concepts of other "self theorists," Kohut for example, were described by Dr. Coltrera as comprising a theory of the self and of the analytic process which is outside "the bounds of the conceptual parsimonies of the psychoanalytic idea" and thus conceptually incompatible with the "classical" tradition. Although he felt that the study of the dyadic relationship and of empathy was valid, Dr. Coltrera cautioned against allowing the use of empathy to lead to a form of "wild analysis." Dr. Phyllis H. Stock suggested that in going back as far as the Medieval and Renaissance periods Dr. Grolnick had complicated his argument. She offered examples of how philosophical terms (e.g., rationalist) have had different meanings in different historical periods. Debates about opposing philosophical viewpoints (such as idealist versus mechanistic, free will versus determinism, rationalism versus empiricism, or even "hard" versus "soft" science) have to be understood within a historical context.

Specialized Techniques in Individual Psychotherapy

Edited by Toksoz B. Karasu, M.D. and Leopold Bellak, M.D. New York: Brunner/Mazel, 1980. 504 pp.

Alex Kaplan

Alex Kaplan

Alex H. Kaplan
ST. LOUIS

Alex Kaplan  

A number of good books dealing with the general subject of psychoanalytically oriented short- and long-term individual psychotherapy have already been published. However, none of them cover the treatment of such a wide range of problems or of the specialized techniques involved in individual psychotherapy as this volume does. Encyclopedic in its range, it covers not only an overview of all psychotherapies and the general principles of psychotherapy, but the application of individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy alone or in combination with other techniques to a wide range of psychiatric conditions.

The book, of great value for the young psychiatric resident and psychiatrist in clinical practice, will also be most helpful to the psychoanalyst and psychiatrist with more clinical experience. The underlying principle throughout this book is the adherence to the psychoanalytic theory of personality and psychopathology as the basis for individual psychotherapy.

[[RunningHead]]

Le Fanatisme. Histoire Et Psychanalyse. (Fanaticism. History and Psychoanalysis.)

By André Haynal, Miklos Molnar, and Gérard de Puymège. Paris: Stock, 1980. 358 pp.

Micheline Levowitz-Treu

Micheline Levowitz-Treu

Micheline Levowitz-Treu
LAKE SUCCESS, N.Y.

Micheline Levowitz-Treu  

No one would dispute that our century has been rich in examples of fanaticism. But what particular events deserve this label? What is the mentality of the fanatic? Or rather, what are the mentalities, since the participants in fanaticism must be divided into two groups, the leaders and the led. What conditions—historical, economic, sociological, political, and/or psychological—allow for the phenomenon to occur? Such are the questions that André Haynal (psychoanalyst), Miklos Molnar (social historian), and Gérard de Puymège (anthropological historian) pose in this book, without necessarily answering them.

In his introduction, Molnar gives an etymological history of the term "fanatic," originating in antiquity, and the term "fanaticism," which dates back only to the eighteenth century. He points out that if, to a great extent, fanaticism makes history, it still cannot be historically defined without the help of other disciplines. Even then, determining the various conditions that have fostered fanaticism in different cultures would be an impossibly complex task. Complex, too, is the question of what behavior constitutes fanaticism. Fanatics need not be fiery zealots. Lenin, for example, was a coldly calculating and well-organized individual. Indeed, this has been true of Communist leaders in general.

In the second section of the book, André Haynal examines fanaticism and civilization from a psychoanalytic perspective: how psychoanalysis defines civilization and how it can help to explain why, how, and where civilization may be undermined by fanaticism. In the third section, de Puymège presents some "cases" of fanaticism, the most interesting of which are taken from French history—the careers of Boulanger and Ravaillac.

The subject is clearly a challenging one, and relatively unexplored. Few studies, in any disciplines, have dealt with fanaticism. A multidisciplinary approach such as this has the advantage of considering the issues from many viewpoints. It also runs the risk of the contributors' holding parallel discourses which do not converge toward a resolution.

Postulating that therapeutic intervention increasing the involvement of the father in parenting would help in treating adolescent borderlines, Anderson has required that fathers (not mothers) be treated concurrently (not conjointly) with the adolescent by the same therapist. He has found this extremely helpful and gives two clinical examples illustrating the advantages and some of the difficulties of this technique. He then reviews the theoretical concept that the presence of an empathic father ("an external object which can survive apart from the mother")

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

Zinner provides a clear, excellent companion paper to that of Shapiro, a member of the same research group. He emphasizes the importance of viewing the whole family of the borderline adolescent as a patient and of presenting this view clearly to the family from the outset. This view is implemented by a treatment approach including: 1) individual treatment of the adolescent by one therapist; 2) conjoint treatment of the parents by a second therapist; and 3) conjoint treatment of the entire family by both, functioning as co-therapists. With the help of case vignettes, he illustrates the difficulties commonly encountered in engaging families in this treatment approach, as well as the therapeutic gains which ensue.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

The author reviews the developmental stage of early adolescence as a time of intensely renewed conflict over separation-individuation. The external environment (e.g., the availability of role models for identification, responses to the adolescent's acting out, social mores, etc.) plays a crucial role in easing or

145

disrupting the developmental processes, particularly of adolescents made more vulnerable by earlier developmental arrests. Miller points out with vivid examples the ways in which our current society at large, as well as common practices in our therapeutic and penal institutions, enhances regression rather than growth and adult resolution in our early adolescents.

The term, acting out, is defined, and the psychoanalytic literature on the concept is reviewed. The author identifies four characteristics which tend to predispose people to act out rather than to verbalize feelings, memories, fantasies, and conflicts. She demonstrates some of these with therapists working to help adolescents reveal and understand the unconscious meanings of their behavior.

Hyperactive Children in Canada and Uganda. A Comparative Evaluation. Klaus K. Minde and Nancy J. Cohen. Pp. 476-487.

Comparisons of the prevalence of psychiatric disorders in different cultures are important in determining the degree to which particular syndromes are culturebound in their manifestations. In this study the authors looked at both clinical evidence and objective measures of behavior with the Peterson-Quay and Rutter Behavior Rating Scales in Canadian and African primary-school-aged children. They conclude that the hyperactive syndrome, albeit in a somewhat different form, occurs in Africa and hence may be a basic deviation in behavior.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. XVII, 1978

Intervention with Overtly Rejecting Parents. A Suggestion for a Collaborative Legal and Psychiatric Approach. Steven A. Frankel. Pp. 498-504.

A review of eighteen cases involving overt parental rejection of a child revealed a strikingly pessimistic prognosis for reconciliation through psychiatric intervention alone. However, the invocation of legal pressure seemed instrumental in motivating the decision of a small number of parents to reconcile with their children. The suggestion is made, therefore, that psychiatric intervention be made early and with conviction, and be joined with a legal intervention if signs of failure become evident.

Manic-Depressive Illness in Adolescence. A Case Report. Frederick W. Engstrom; Douglas R. Robbins; J. Gary May. Pp. 514-520.

A case report of manic-depressive illness in a fifteen-year-old girl is presented, with a discussion of the diagnostic and therapeutic issues which are raised. The

147

patient was previously well adjusted and then suffered one depressive and two manic attacks in one year. Her mania responded well to treatment with lithium carbonate, but it recurred briefly when the lithium level fell to subtherapeutic levels. She has been asymptomatic for the two years since then. Manic-depressive illness may be underdiagnosed in adolescents in the United States.

A Comparison of Abused Children and Their Nonabused Siblings. Ellen C. Herrenkohl and Roy C. Herrenkohl. Pp. 260-269.

Two hundred ninety-five targets of abuse were compared to two hundred eighty-four nonabused siblings with reference to birth record data and maternal perceptions of the birth and subsequent development of the child. Prematurity, Apgar scores, age of mother at child's birth, self-reports of postpartum depression,

149

maternal perceptions of emotional difficulties of the child, of the child's ability to be influenced by the mother, and of negative characteristics of the child reminiscent of others were related to certain types of abuse and gross neglect. Explanatory hypotheses include weakened attachment bonds and maternal projection of negative attributes and feelings of helplessness.

Child-Abusing Fathers. Arthur H. Green. Pp. 270-282.

Typical personality traits, psychodynamics, and environmental influences are described in eight child-abusing fathers. Paternal child abuse is usually accompanied by simrultaneous abuse of the spouse and excessive drinking. A history of maternal deprivation and unresolved dependency on the spouse are key psychodynamic issues shared by this population. Based on the data presented, a rationale for psychiatric intervention and treatment of child-abusing fathers is suggested.

Violent Juvenile Delinquents. Psychiatric, Neurological, Psychological, and Abuse Factors. Dorothy Otnow Lewis, et al. Pp. 307-319.

This study compares the neuropsychiatric, intellectual, and educational status of extremely violent and less violent incarcerated boys. The more violent children were more likely to demonstrate psychotic symptomatology (paranoid ideation and rambling, illogical associations) and to have major and minor neurological abnormalities. They were also more likely to have experienced and witnessed extreme physical abuse. The contribution of these factors to violent delinquency is discussed, and implications for therapeutic intervention are suggested.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. XVIII, 1979

Psychotherapeutic Issues in the Treatment of Sexually Abused Girls. Katherine MacVicar. Pp. 342-353.

Experience in treating both accidental and participating victims of sexual assault suggests that while most of the adolescent accidental victims responded well to crisis intervention therapy, both of the latency accidental victims and all of the participating victims required a much longer period of therapy to obtain any relief of symptoms. Long-term therapy was characterized by much testing of the therapist, either in the form of seductive behaviors in the case of male therapists or in the form of aggressively provocative behaviors in the case of female therapists. The most common symptoms encountered in latency children were phobias, behavior disorders, and learning disturbances, while in adolescents depression was most often seen.

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

April 16, 1979. COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT AND FEMALE PSYCHOLOGY. Martin A. Silverman, M.D.

Dr. Silverman stated that the core gender identity of the girl begins to form as soon as her parents recognize her as female. Parents handle, react, and speak differently to their male and female offspring, who show demonstrable sensory, motor, responsive, and other sex-related differences at birth. As a result of on-going interaction with their parents, little girls build up a concept of their gender identity that is stable by three years of age or sooner. Vaginal awareness does not appear to be a significant factor in the evolution of a girl's core gender identity in early life. The mother's feelings toward the girl and her femaleness, as well as toward herself and her own femaleness, contribute to the child's initial views of and feelings about herself and to transformations which occur in those views and feelings. A little girl's self concept about being a girl is also greatly influenced by what her father conveys to her about the way he views her and what he expects of her.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Manuel Furer saw in Dr. Winestine's work a creative combination of the ideas of Aichhorn, Loewald, and Mahler. However, he disagreed with the position taken by the author. He suggested that the primary trauma was the mother's depression, as well as the various losses and rejections the child was confronting. A central conflict such as this can serve to organize ensuing traumata; thus the accidental fall down the stairs was significant because it fit in with a central conflict. Although the first phase of the therapy was more in line with usual psychoanalytic principles, it nevertheless was colored by the author's bias. This bias is, of course, explicit in the second phase and forms the main thesis of her paper. Dr. Furer was unable to see that a change in technique was indicated and maintained that a consistent and persistent interpretation of the various manifestations of the patient's conflicts remained the best approach.

Dr. Theodore Shapiro asserted that when one writes such a case report, the material is ordered according to what one knows, e.g., according to a set of preconceived cognitive organizations known as theory—the theory in this case being Dr. Mahler's separation-individuation theory. This theory is used by Dr. Winestine in her work to complement the usual classical analytic mode and is especially evident in the phase of the treatment where she attempted to foster the building of structure and the overcoming of developmental arrests. Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

October 16, 1979. THE ORAL DRIVE, CLINGING, AND EQUILIBRIUM. Lester Friedman, M.D.

Dr. Friedman described the various symptoms of disequilibrium (dizziness, lightheadedness, etc.) as observed in patients in analysis. He reviewed the theories relating such phenomena to sexual excitement, regression to preoedipal states (Isakower), and other explanations and then offered one of his own: under certain circumstances there can be a revival of the disequilibratory aspect of the experience of abrupt interruption of nursing, which entails interruption not only of oral gratification but also of the associated clinging to the maternal object. He described the close genetic relationship between sucking and clinging, with the object of demonstrating the linkage between sucking, clinging, and disequilibratory symptoms in response to the movements attendant upon being removed (especially suddenly) from the feeding situation. He then cited a detailed clinical example of disequilibrium arising in an analysand when regular attendance at sessions was interrupted by the analyst's canceling two sessions. The disequilibrium occurred when the analyst interpreted the patient's defensive acting out as an effort to avoid experiencing the analyst as abandoning him. The patient had many memories of separations from his mother early in life and of turning to his father for contact. There was much evidence of the patient's disappointment with his mother as someone he could not cling to. Dr. Friedman described his belief that the form of the symptom and its context support the hypothesis that, under the impact of the transference, there had been a revival of the disequilibratory aspect of actual experiences of abruptly interrupted feeding-clinging in infancy. This was supported by the picture of the mother emerging in the analysis as aggressively controlling and depriving, with a dislike for holding babies. There were other aspects of the immediate associations as well, which Dr. Friedman considered to be related to the same archaic situation, although the specific memory that was recovered was of a paternal figure playing with him at the age of four by throwing him in the air. The dizziness recurred at a time in the analysis when there was a libidinal progressive movement (thoughts of marrying). There was repeated evidence of response to castration anxiety by wishing to be fed. In addition, the patient had a castrative urge toward the analyst, whose holiday with his family he envied, and there were primal scene dreams in association with actual contacts with his mother.

Asher Rosenberg

Asher Rosenberg

Asher Rosenberg  

DISCUSSION: Dr. S. Warren Seides mentioned Freud's strongly held view that religion is a neurotic compromise which creates the illusion of a protecting father. The developmental level of the instinctual wishes involved in the compromise were seen by Freud as phallic-oedipal, and the objects of these wishes were seen as whole objects. Dr. Seides emphasized that preoedipal experiences, component instincts, and part objects can appear as part of religious and mythological symbols in the content of the later thoughts without being central to the origin of the symbol or to its current meaning. In determining genetic origins, timing is essential. Dr. Seides felt that Dr. Almansi had first defined several symbols as they appear in myth and religion and then had retrospectively placed their importance in the preverbal period. The Tetragrammaton and the Tables of the Law could plausibly symbolize other parts of the body. For example, the Tetragrammaton could represent a phallus, and the Tables of the Law could represent breasts, a face, a couple, or genitals. Thus different interpretations of the symbol could place its origin in a later developmental phase. Furthermore, symbolization is not thought to occur before twenty-two to thirty months of age, which is long after the preverbal stage. The punitive aspects of the hands in religious symbolism is consistent with later superego development and difficult to attribute to the infant in the symbiotic stage. The oceanic feeling of being one with the world, which relates to early experiences with the mother, was not considered by Freud to be a source of religious needs. Dr. Seides concluded that "oedipal level ambivalence, rather than preverbal experiences, seems more productive of the deterministic, causative mode of thinking in religious and mythological belief systems." Dr. Nathaniel Ross agreed with Dr. Almansi on the importance of exploring the nature of the earliest inner experiences of infants. Systematic observations reported in the literature indicate that the infant responds to the sensory stimuli provided by the parents from the earliest moments of life and that these sensory experiences have a lasting influence on the development of the infant. Experiments with infant animals demonstrate the impact of early sensory experience not only on behavior but on later brain chemistry, neurophysiology, and endocrinological functions as well. These studies correlate suggestively with Dr. Almansi's impression that preverbal perceptions contribute significantly to the development of the psyche and to mythological and religious phenomena. Dr. Ross emphasized the disparate, fluctuating nature of the infant's experiences in the earliest years before the integration of part self and part object representations.

Lothar W.—Klaus Holzkamp's Most Famous Case. Christian Niemeyer. Pp. 306-342.

The group organized around Klaus Holzkamp has developed a theoretical-therapeutic conception of "critical psychology." This involves overextending the categorical framework of Marx's critique of political economy so as to derive insights for a science of subjectivity. In this effort the relevance of the life-historical dimension, which is decisive in psychoanalysis, is systematically rejected in favor of the influence of social factors. Pathology is conceptualized as a deficient capacity for insight into social conditions and into the possibilities of the praxis of change.

Hilda Rollman-Branch

Hilda S. Rollman-Branch
LOS ANGELES

Hilda Rollman-Branch  

This French work contains the written presentations and conclusions of the "Haslemere Symposium," which took place in 1976. For this reviewer it would have been easier to read the various articles in their original languages, because the translations into French are more difficult to understand than the original French contributions, an interesting lesson in itself and an indication of how closely language is related to identity. Nevertheless, I feel it will be valuable to offer the following necessarily brief surveys of the papers to convey the gist of the major emphases of the symposium. I will include related observations of my own.

Discussing "the identity of the psychoanalyst," Edward D. Joseph refers to the establishment of a stable self-representation as a result of the separation-individuation phase and to Erikson's concept of a sense of identity at the end of adolescence. He notes that the definition of personal identity includes a sense of continuity in relation to past, present, and future.

The sense of a psychoanalytic identity develops gradually from the identifications with training analyst, supervisors, teachers, and colleagues.

By Joseph Goldstein, Anna Freud, and Albert J. Solnit. New York: The Free Press, 1979. 288 pp.

Aaron Esman

Aaron H. Esman
NEW YORK

Aaron Esman  

In 1973, Solnit, Freud, and Goldstein launched upon the intersecting worlds of medicine, law, and social welfare a literary bombshell whose reverberations are still audible. Their earlier book, Beyond the Best Interests of the Child,1 was a penetrating, relentlessly lucid examination of the ways in which society managed—and mismanaged—the lives of children. It proposed a formula—"the least damaging alternative"—to guide the legal agencies of our society in their pursuit of what had been, until then, the rather vague doctrine of "the best interests of the child." Their reasoning was based, throughout, on the application of psychoanalytic developmental psychology to the complex issues that beset child custody, foster care, adoption, and residential placement, in all of which, it was assumed, the state had both the right and the necessity to intervene.

Now, the same authors address themselves to the prior question: When, how, and under what circumstances should and may the state intervene in the lives of children? Guided by their own basic principle of the relative inviolability of the parent-child relationship, they argue forcefully and with implacable logic in support of what they call here "the least intrusive intervention.

Basic Handbook of Child Psychiatry

Edited by Joseph D. Noshpitz, et al. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1979. Vol. I: Development, 729 pp; Vol. II: Disturbances of Development, 749 pp; Vol. III: Therapeutic Interventions, 704 pp; Vol. IV: Prevention and Current Issues, 696 pp.

H. Blank

H. Blank

H. Robert Blank
WHITE PLAINS, N.Y.

H. Blank  

The editors and two hundred and fifty contributors have produced the most exhaustive, creatively organized, and engaging reference work in child psychiatry. It covers the age spectrum from conception to twenty years. No facet of the subject, no interdisciplinary linkage, has been neglected. This is perhaps best exemplified by the splendid Chapter 3, in Vol. I, "The Molecular Biology of Development" by J. Gerald Young and Donald J. Cohen. They present the essentials of human genetics, neurochemistry, and neuroendocrinology which are related to the concepts of stress and trauma and to intrapsychic, interpersonal, and social factors.

There are major differences in theoretical orientation and practice in the big and expanding field of child psychiatry. The editors have dealt candidly and instructively with these differences in their wise selection of authors and in their own discussions. There is considerable variation in the quality of writing and depth of coverage of the assigned topics. Very few of the contributions are inadequate—the bulk of them are most praiseworthy.

Many contributions throughout the Handbook—not all by psychoanalysts—explicitly and implicitly indicate the major influence of psychoanalysis in the early and continuing development of child psychiatry. An impressive number of psychoanalysts engaged in practice, teaching, and research in child psychiatry are among the editors and other contributors; for example: Sidney Berman, Rudolf Ekstein, Robert Emde, Stuart Finch, Eleanor Galenson, Sally Provence, Herman Roiphe, and Albert J. Solnit.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Pankow has developed a psychoanalytic psychotherapy of the psychoses which emphasizes the body image. Psychosis consists of the destruction of the fundamental symbolic structures which contain the first experiences of the body. In neurosis, these symbolic structures are deformed rather than destroyed. Pankow uses "dynamic structuralization" to intervene with psychotic patients in this process of destruction. In her technique she focuses on a potential space which was important in the development of a sense of separateness from the mother. Theoretical justifications for her technical innovations are presented. She feels that her work deals with phenomena similar to Winnicott's transitional objects. This potential space is often left out of consideration in classical psychoanalysis. There are many paradoxes and difficulties in the theoretical characterization of such intermediate phenomena. The question has been raised whether a new structural theory might be needed to accommodate these phenomena.

Concerning the Primary Seizure in Essential Epilepsy. Colette Guédeney. Pp. 303-324.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Guédeney relies on clinical material gathered over several years by a multidisciplinary team. She attempts to understand in psychoanalytic terms the first seizure in cases of essential epilepsy in which there is no evident neurological lesion. She finds that these first seizures have much in common. In general they

296

occur in early childhood in a context of psychic tensions for the individual and for the family, and they are most often preceded by a decisive event. Hence the economic factor is of major importance. The defenses of the ego are precarious in the face of intense drive tensions. The psychological elements in such a seizure are projection, failure of repression, and failure of symbolization. The ego is forced to resort to primitive defense mechanisms such as destructuralizing, regression, and splitting. This splitting involves the loss of consciousness and amnesia for the seizure. The epileptic is forced into a quasi-biological regression and attempts to flee from the threatened danger by this regression. A comparison with dreams and with the hysterical attack is helpful. The regression in epilepsy goes far beyond the hallucinatory wish fulfillment of the dream experience and returns to fixation points probably preceding the formation of the ego. In contrast to hysterical attacks, there is a complete failure of symbolization.

297

A Study of the Psychoanalytic Signifier in Freud's Case Histories. Nicos Nicolaïdis and François Corun. Pp. 325-350.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

This linguistically oriented article contrasts the linguistic signifier with the psychoanalytic signifier. A signifier, for de Saussure, contained the signified as a concept. The psychoanalytic signifier, however, has the instinctual representative as its content. With this claim in mind, the authors study Freud's five case histories for the use he makes of psychoanalytically important signifiers, such as the word "rat" in the Rat Man case. They claim that Freud made enormous use of this linguistic characteristic to enable him to understand the unconscious conflicts of the individuals he studied.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Guédeney compares rhetorical figures of speech (e.g., metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche) with displacement, condensation, and representability. She feels that the latter bear witness to the functioning of the psychic apparatus just as the figures bear witness to the existence of language. There is no discourse without these figures of speech, just as there is no mental activity without condensation, displacement, etc. The unconscious structures language and constitutes it. From language comes syntax, the notion of time, contradiction, and difference. These tropes are not created ex nihilo, but result from the work of the unconscious and show the abilities of the unconscious thought processes. All the tropes have a symbolic value and permit one to hear something other than what is said.

"Depressivity" and Depression in the Framework of the Economics of Defense. Jean Bergeret. Pp. 835-1044.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Bergeret considers the economic differences which separate "depressivity" from actual depression. "Depressivity" or the "essential depressive" seems to correspond to the depressive personality organization. Depressivity constitutes a defense as much against the failure of narcissistic counterinvestments as against perceived threats of object loss. By this the author means that there is a difficulty in preserving an internal object, in addition to a difficulty in abandoning the relationship with an external object and mourning for its loss. As a defensive organization, depressivity results in characterological compromises which are often long-lasting and which can succeed, more or less, in maintaining self-esteem and object idealization sufficient to permit adequate functioning and sometimes even to incite a certain level of restorative creativity. Yet the functioning is barely adequate, and there is vulnerability to decompensation and actual depression. The anal-receptive phase of development is very important.

Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

Is the Dream a Wish-Fulfillment? Comments on the Relation between Hermeneutics and Theory in Freud's "Interpretation of Dreams." Martin Bartels. Pp. 97-131.

Bartels sees Freud's method of dream interpretation as essentially hermeneutic: the awakened dreamer, motivated by his interest in restoring the unitary meaning of his life and in preserving his identity, seeks to integrate the alien dream experience into his self-understanding. The "meaning" of the dream, constituted in the dream report, is realized in the extension of the dreamer's self-understanding and in the re-establishment of his identity, which are brought about and validated in the interpretive dialogue. The truth of the interpretation lies in its biographically efficacious application. Yet Freud inquires not merely about the meaning of the dream, but also about its function; he adds a functional psychological explanation to the interpretation. The critical departure from the direct understanding of dreams and waking life, the skeptical devaluation of the manifest dream content in favor of the interpreted latent dream thought, and the emphasis on the resistance to interpretation, rather than the wish to interpret—all of these appear as inconsistencies within the hermeneutic program and as compromises with (nonpsychological) scientific conceptions.

The author shows the untenability of the simple assumption that poetic fiction is determined by the male or female author's sex-specific daydreams. James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

These extremely rich articles need careful reading to do justice to the authors' scholarly productions. Psychoanalytic metapsychology has pursued an erratic course as a result of external changes which are a reflection of the larger changes in twentieth-century science. Through an understanding of this relatively simple observation, the author suggests, it is quite possible to harmonize psychology and physics, "within a new and more comprehensive natural philosophy or scientific 'world-picture.'" Thus the mind-body dichotomy is seen as a result of the zig-zag path along which both philosophy and science have developed since the seventeenth century, and it is not in any way related to the development of clinical psychoanalysis. The author believes that we have now amassed enough data to bridge what was at one time an irreconcilable dichotomy. Ricoeur acknowledges the significance of Toulmin's work but questions whether we are really able at this time to resolve the mind-body problem. Swanson disagrees with Toulmin in that he does not see how mind-body complementarity relates to quantum mechanical complementarity. He feels that while Toulmin's arguments are significant, there is not enough evidence to back them up.

The possibility of creative instances exists in everyone's life. Precursors of such creative instances are thought to include periods of searching, preparation, incubation, regression, and altered levels of consciousness. The psychotherapist may in his work encounter such creativity as an affective experience, the "Aha!" phenomenon. Kubie spoke of "creative invention," the essential process being the uncovering of new facts and especially of new relationships among both new and old data. The clinician's creative behavior may consist of his selecting the favorable content and timing for a confrontation or interpretation. Because the creative and neurotic processes may be intertwined, the possibility for creativity may correspond to the degree of freedom from neurosis. Rather than viewing creativity as an esoteric quality of genius, the author feels that with the right stimuli and motivations, most clinicians are afforded instances of participation in the creative process.

Conscious recall of primal scene exposure was elicited in interviews with fifty college-age persons. Their reactions were viewed from three perspectives: the psychoanalytic model (emphasizing libidinal affects and feelings of danger), the existential (emphasizing feelings of aloneness and exclusion with loss of security, rather than sexuality), and the cognitive-affective (emphasizing the effect of the child's inability to understand what he has seen). On the basis of this consciously elicited data, the author concludes that primal scene stimulation usually produces long-term traumatic effects only if it has occurred within a context of generalized brutality and markedly disturbed family relationships. Primal scene exposure may even be beneficial in stimulating healthy curiosity about the "facts of life," sexual activity, and reassurances about the bondedness of the parents.

Stressful Life Events and Community Mental Health Center Patients. Daniel Mueller; Daniel Edwards; Richard Yarvis. Pp. 16-24.

The first of these papers is a review article with suggestions for further research. Of particular interest are the criticisms of many studies of the relationship between stressful life events and subsequent illness. The authors show how oversimplified are the cause-and-effect notions underlying conclusions that the stressful life event itself is the cause of the psychological illness. For example, disturbance subsequent to an accident or divorce has been all too frequently interpreted as the consequence of the stressful event itself, rather than being primarily related to the pathology which in turn contributed to the development of the stressful event. The second paper illustrates the thesis propounded by the first. In a sample of patients from a community mental health center there was actually no greater incidence of stressful life events before treatment than in a control group, when the events which were probably a consequence of their psychological disturbance were eliminated from the total.

Richter's widely cited experiments with swimming rats (Psychosom. Med., 1957) were interpreted as showing that the affects of hopelessness and helplessness caused wild rats swimming in a cylinder to give up, enter a parasympathetically mediated withdrawal response, and allow themselves to drown. The Psychohistory Review. VII, No. 4, 1979

Belenski and Bakunin: A Psychological Study of Adolescence in 19th Century Russia. Patrick P. Dunn. Pp. 17-23.

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley

Peter Buckley  

The adolescence of Belenski and Bakunin, two of the seminal figures of nineteenth century Russian intellectual life, is examined in this paper. Both repudiated tradition, authority, and custom during their passage through adolescence, and both embraced German idealism. This philosophy provided for the two young intellectuals a convenient structure within which their asceticism could be rationalized. In Belenski's case the resolution of adolescent conflicts resulted in his acceptance of his sexual impulses and enabled him eventually to marry and begin his illustrious literary career. In contrast, Bakunin remained in a state of prolonged adolescence and hence was unable to consummate a relationship with a woman. Throughout his adult life he continued to indulge in grandiose fantasies of limitless possibilities in life. Bakunin's revolutionary schemes never became more than fantasies while in Belenski's case, he was able to transform the defensive operations of adolescence into adaptive ones, become a husband and father, and ultimately a major figure in Russian social and intellectual history.

A developmental assessment of the ego capacities of the children and parents of disorganized families gives one a basis for understanding the family members' adaptive capacities and areas of psychosocial malfunctioning. The assessment also permits a task-oriented approach toward helping family members attempt to remediate individual and family conflicts. The co-therapists' work and the close monitoring of the family's efforts at task completion are described. A developmental task-oriented approach has been successful in effecting durable behavior changes in members of a number of disorganized families.

When autonomous rights cannot be exercised by an individual because that person is comatose, mentally retarded, mentally ill, or a child, a surrogate exercises this power through proxy consent. The traditional choice of the family as proxy for children is under attack. The concept of relative competence

459

is an alternative to determinations of competence or incompetence. Proxy consent involves not only deciding who speaks for the child but defining who needs proxies. Psychiatrists must familiarize themselves with the issues, in such concepts as autonomy, autonomous rights, consent, competence, surrogation of authority, representation, paternalism versus individuality, and the hierarchy of values.

A nine-year-old Puerto Rican boy with agenesis of the testicles provided an unusual opportunity to explore the role of the testicles in psychosexual development. The recent literature on the psychological role of the testicles is reviewed. This case report demonstrates that the patient experienced the absence of testicles as a phallic defect. Identical Twins Simultaneously Concordant for Anorexia Nervosa. Random C. Simmons and Mina D. Kessler. Pp. 527-536.

Identical twin girls, whose monozygosity was determined by blood group analysis, simultaneously developed anorexia nervosa at the age of eleven. Treatment consisting of individual, outpatient, insight-oriented psychotherapy for each girl by separate therapists, and work with the parents by a social worker, uncovered significant conflict in the area of identity formation, apparently exacerbated by the twinship. Resolution of the anorexia and significant ego growth in both twins rapidly followed exploration of the twinship dynamics in therapy. Gains made during the relatively brief therapy were well maintained at a two-year follow-up evaluation.

The literature on adolescent breast development is reviewed, including the physiological sequence of normal female adolescent breast development and the psychological responses of the adolescent, her family, and her peers to such development. Breast development is a line of developmental growth neglected by psychiatrists, pediatricians, and other health professionals. It is critical that those dealing with adolescents both note and discuss with the female her feelings about her physical development in relationship to herself, her peers (male and female), and her family.

Ego Development and Interpersonal Style in Adolescence. Stuart T. Hauser. Pp. 333-352.

In psychodynamic psychiatry and psychoanalysis, the concept of ego development is important for both clinical and theoretical work. It has been difficult, however, to derive techniques which meaningfully measure ego development for use in clinical research. The Loevinger Sentence Completion Test has been found reliable and valid, but no study has shown it directly pertinent to clinical perspectives. Our research investigated clinically relevant correlates of ego development, using the Loevinger test followed by videotaped interviews of ninety-eight adolescent girls, to discover how certain character styles predicted to be associated with different ego levels would be expressed in interpersonal interactions. Our results were consistent with clinical and theoretical descriptions of adolescents from varying ego development levels. These findings emphasize the relevance and usefulness of the ego development measure for clinical research and studies of the life cycle.

Adolescent Life Changes and Illness: A Comparison of Three Models. Gerald T. Hotaling; Saundra G. Atwell; Arnold S. Linsky. Pp. 393-403.

This article examines how stressful life events relate to the occurrence of illness in a nonclinical random sample of adolescents and what processes intervene in this relationship. Three alternative models of the life events and illness relationship are compared. Data support a "direct stress and illness model" as opposed to either a "sick role behavior model" or a "mental health model." Social support from parents appears to mediate the life events-illness relationship. Undesirable and ambiguous life events have more impact on illness than desirable events. Results are discussed in terms of adolescence as a unique developmental stage.

of identity status, intimacy status, and self-esteem. Males were found to focus on intrapersonal aspects of identity, females on interpersonal aspects. Theoretical discussions of adolescence tend to emphasize the importance of physical development, self-views, and a traditional aspect of adolescence. The view that black youth frequently manifest disordered personalities and negative self-concepts is examined through a comparison of the responses of black and white female adolescents from differing cultural and social class backgrounds to an Adjective Check List. While their responses were dissimilar from those of white female adolescents in many important respects, black subjects scored high on indices of personal adjustment and did not describe themselves in negatively valued terms. In fact, black girls from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, who are generally portrayed as particularly prone to pathology and negative self-evaluations, describe themselves in more favorable terms than black and white subjects from middle class backgrounds. Moreover, United States and Jamaican black subjects describe themselves in surprisingly similar fashion and differ in similar respects from their white American counterparts, thereby providing some evidence for the impact of a common cultural heritage on black personality cross-nationally.

The Effects of the Yom Kippur War on Values of Israeli Female Students. Ron Hoz and Mordecai Nisan. Pp. 161-169.

The Rokeach Terminal Value Scale and an attitude questionaire were administered to two similar groups of female Israeli students before and after the Yom Kippur War. The second group also responded to a questionnaire about the effects of the war on the importance attributed to each of the values. The results were as follows: (a) Subjects stated that after the war, fourteen out of the eighteen values in the Rokeach list increased in importance. (b) The war brought about a significant increase in the relative importance (rank) of four values (pleasure, national security, happiness, and mature love) and a significant decrease in rank for equality. (c) No attitude change was found in respect to issues related to the war itself. (d) Values accounted for a smaller per cent of the variance in attitudes after the war than they did before it. In view of these findings it is suggested that a distinction be made between relative and absolute importance within a value system.

November 27, 1979. BUILDING A CLINICAL THEORY: THE SCIENCE OF OUR ART (Abraham A. Brill Memorial Lecture). Walter A. Stewart, M.D.

The quest for an integration of theory and practice was the touchstone of Dr. Stewart's lecture. Beginning with a historical review, he reminded the audience that Freud's earliest writings smoothly integrated a theory, albeit a simple one, of the mind, neurosis, and treatment. Symptoms resulting from strangulated affects were relieved by the recall of repressed unconscious memories. Following the discovery of infantile sexuality, a far more complex view of the mind evolved. A greater appreciation of the roles of insight, reconstruction, and working through extended psychoanalysis beyond symptom removal to the more comprehensive treatment of the individual. Dr. Stewart explored the still elusive aspects of the therapeutic experience. How does the analytic process bring about good results? What is the science of our art? To address this question, Dr. Stewart turned to an evolutionary view and a developmental frame of reference, emphasizing the interrelation of biological maturation, drives, ego development, and the modifying effect of the environment. In this evolutionary process the individual, somewhat freed of reflex action through the use of thought, nonetheless becomes more susceptible to psychoneurosis. Dr. Stewart repeatedly emphasized the importance of the role of the ego and its functions, and how its resolution of tasks determines character. Failure in the resolution of childhood conflicts leads to endless repetition of maladaptive responses. The goal of therapy goes beyond the cure of symptoms through understanding their meaning and beyond interpreting conflicts elicited in dreams and by free association. "The discovery of the actual deleterious experiences in order to understand the damage they have inflicted on development is necessary."

Dr. Stewart outlined the psychosexual stages of development as they unfold in relation to caretaking figures and become encoded in memories. The consequences of a less than adequate mother-infant relationship leads inevitably to poor self-object differentiation and to character traits of greed, mistrust, chronic complaining, depression, and paranoia, according to Dr. Stewart. Further self-object differentiation through the anal phase encompasses the experiences centering on control and domination. Toilet training is but a part of this phase of development. Throughout, Dr. Stewart shifted from the historically earlier psychoanalytic emphasis on the instincts to an emphasis on ego conflicts which emerge during development and which are then linked to later editions of the same conflicts. Thus the Wolf Man's feeling financially discriminated against in relation to his sister in later life was partly his reliving of childhood feelings of being cheated of his full share of birthday gifts.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Phyllis Greenacre emphasized other aspects of the possible meaning of the padlock. She indicated that the secret padlock might reflect the many aspects of Dr. Johnson's polymorphous perverse tendencies. It could be a fetish used as part of sadomasochistic beating fantasies or activities, as well as a warning of the danger of madness which he feared might result from his compulsive masturbation. It seemed a symbol, too, of his love for Mrs. Thrale and his trust in her to help him and to keep secret the nature of his difficulties. Dr. Greenacre also emphasized the intricacy of his relationship to both Mr. and Mrs. Thrale, a situation which was revealed only by Mr. Thrale's illness and death. Dr. Stuart Feder presented five criteria which he felt are required for a responsible psychoanalytic approach to biography: parsimony, coherence, generation, comprehensiveness, and objectivity. By generation he meant the ability of the insights attained to accommodate new elements of biographical detail. Objectivity refers to the utilization of subjective responses as a tool for the achievement of insight. Dr. Feder praised Dr. Meyer's paper and demonstrated how it had met his criteria. He did question whether literary works could be equated with fantasy and also suggested that for "Dictionary Johnson" words themselves may have become erotized. Thus, the use of certain words, such as "rod" and "padlock," by him and Mrs. Thrale may have produced partial but perhaps adequate discharge of his perverse wishes.

In order to further understand which types of family interactions help children to mature optimally, over one hundred fifty family groups were methodically interviewed and observed. Although seriously dysfunctional families tended to produce troubled children, no significant differences in adolescents' functioning could be found between children of "optimal" and of "competent but pained" families. "Optimal" families consisted of parents who could be very close to each other and to their children without sacrifice of individuality. These families were highly expressive of all feelings and these expressions were met with empathic responses. "Competent but pained" familiess shared some of these characteristics but differed in the quality of interaction between parents. There was less empathy and more unresolved conflict within the parental relationship.

Emotion, Thought and Therapy. A Study of Hume and Spinoza and the Relationship of Philosophical Theories of the Emotions to Psychological Theories of Therapy

By Jerome Neu. Berkeley/Los Angeles: University of California Press, 1977. 194 pp.

Bennett Simon

Bennett Simon

Bennett Simon
WEST NEWTON, MASS.

Bennett Simon  

This book is a major contribution to our understanding of the relationship between problems in philosophy of thought and problems

447

in psychoanalysis around the nature of thought and emotion. The argument of the book begins with an extended contrast between Hume and Spinoza on the nature of emotions. This contrast is between "systematic representatives of two opposing traditions of argument about the relation of thought and feeling in the emotions. The Humeans treat emotions as essentially feelings (impressions or affects) with thoughts incidentally attached. The Spinozists say roughly the reverse, treating emotions as essentially thoughts ('ideas' or 'beliefs') with feelings incidentally attached" (p. 152). Spinoza, the author argues, is closer to the truth, and, further, Spinoza's position represents a position closer to the premises of psychoanalysis.

This bare outline scarcely does justice to the richness, subtlety, and importance of this book. The author is a professional philosopher whose interests center on "philosophy of mind," a philosopher who has a profound understanding of many aspects of psychoanalytic thought. His analysis of Hume and Spinoza is a detailed study of the question of how affects are embedded in, and in part defined by, belief and thought. This question, in turn, is crucial for a consideration of several fundamental psychoanalytic questions, e.g., how interpretations effect emotional changes, the nature of insight, the problem of unconscious affects, and how fantasy may affect somatic processes.

The contrast between Hume (Chapter I) and Spinoza (Chapter II) forms the basis for Chapter III, "Thought, Theory and Therapy," the chapter most explicitly dealing with psychoanalytic issues. There, Neu produces an extraordinarily interesting analysis of the contrast between psychoanalytic and nonpsychoanalytic therapies (especially behavioral therapy).

For me, a most important contribution of this book is the application of Spinoza's ideas on transforming emotions via understanding to the goal of increasing the individual's freedom to act and to choose. In contrast to Hume's, Spinoza's constructions seem to allow for processes of change in the intensity, object, and causes of the emotions. He provides a framework compatible with the nuanced consideration of emotions demanded by clinical data. Further, Spinoza's views of the complexities of emotions are compatible with data about the cultural and historical patterning of emotions, which are clearly biologically embedded.
