This short article attempts to overcome the destructive polarization in psychoanalysis today between those who characterize psychoanalysis as a branch of the humanities and those who designate it a science. The author proposes that "Bohr's epistemological device of complementarity" can be used to resolve this problem. He demonstrates that it is not enough to be concerned with the meaning of things, as for instance Schafer is, since the basis of psychoanalysis concerns affects; without understanding the affectual component, the meaning of things themselves is meaningless. In this context he very succinctly summarizes the problem: "… affects signify simultaneously what is historically meaningful and what is or has been biologically purposeful." Thus, to return to the author's original assertion, complementarity prevents the polarization between psychoanalysis as a science and psychoanalysis as a branch of the humanities.

Two experiments were conducted to examine the development of cardiovascular correlates of attention in normal children and young adults. In the first experiment, heart rate, blood pressure, and peripheral blood flow were measured, and peripheral vascular resistance was calculated while normal college-aged students (seventeen to twenty-three years) were engaged in various psychological tasks. Changes in the cardiovascular indices appeared to reflect the degree of personal meaningfulness and the direction of attention (inward versus outward). In the second experiment, school-aged children (ages nine to twelve years) were monitored while engaged in interviews, watching television, and performing a simple reaction-time task. The neutral interview and the reaction-time task elicited external direction of attention and sensory intake, associated with increased peripheral resistance and decreased peripheral blood flow. The children and the adults differed in their responses to the more personal interview and the reaction-time task. These differences in response may reflect developmental processes.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. VIII, 1979

The Adolescent Sexual Asphyxia Syndrome. Stephen Rosenblum and Myron M. Faber. Pp. 546-558.

The syndrome of self-hanging while masturbating to achieve sexual gratification is known as "sexual asphyxia." Its origins are obscure, but probably date back to the 1600's. The syndrome accounts for at least two hundred fifty deaths per year in the United States alone. Reported victims range in age from eleven to well over sixty years, but most are adolescents. Though typically perceived as happy, well-adjusted people, they are found hanging by the neck, often wearing women's clothing, apparently having died while masturbating. Few living practitioners have been interviewed. The case report of one is presented here. A developmental model is proposed to explicate the differences and similarities between adolescent and adult practitioners.

Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

February 26, 1980. DR. JOHNSON'S SECRET PADLOCK. Bernard C. Meyer, M.D.

Samuel Johnson suffered periods of severe depression marked by lethargy, intense feelings of guilt, and various preoccupations, the nature of which were taken up by Dr. Meyer. Johnson feared that he would become permanently insane. He suffered a prolonged depression, starting in 1759 at the time of his mother's death, from which he obtained relief only in 1765 when he was taken into the home of a couple who befriended him, Mr. and Mrs. Thrale. He lived intermittently in their home until shortly before the end of his life. By then, Mr. Thrale had died, and Mrs. Thrale had remarried, leaving Johnson broken-hearted. Shortly after his arrival Johnson had given this lady a padlock, the existence of which came to light many years later. Basing his ideas on a 1949 paper by Katherine Balderston, entitled "Johnson's Vile Melancholy," Dr. Meyer suggested that behind Johnson's possession of the padlock lay a perverse sexual organization in which bondage was a central element. He summarized two of Johnson's literary works: Rasselas, written at the time of his mother's death, and The Fountain, a fairy tale. In each, the protagonist seeks to escape a confinement which is at the same time portrayed as desirable. Johnson was also preoccupied with beatings. In her diary, Mrs. Thrale quoted him as saying, "… a Woman has such power … that she may tye a Man to a post and whip him if she will." At a later date Mrs. Thrale added in the margin: "This he knew of himself was literally and strictly true I am sure.

Downey explores the links between Winnicott's concept of transitional areas and Freud's (1924) view on the discovery of the object in the external world. Both concepts suggest permanent residuals in reality testing. This paper is based on adolescent analysis and the patient's "transitional" attitudes toward food, clothing, and setting as calibration of oedipal and preoedipal levels and transference. Two cases are presented.

Trauma and Affects. Henry Krystal. Pp. 81-116.

Michael Trupp

Michael Trupp

Michael Trupp  

This paper is a theoretical study of psychic trauma which differentiates "massive infantile trauma (Freud's todesangst; Stern's "biotrauma") from more common "near-trauma" states observed in adults. The full-blown traumatic state is seen initially in adults as ego surrender to unavoidable danger; it is followed by a specific regressive series: anxiety, catatonic state, aphanesis (phylogenetically programmed "self-destruct" mechanism), and psychogenic death. In both forms, affective intolerance and constrictive character result.

The Nature of Adolescent Pathology and the Psychoanalytic Process. Moses Laufer. Pp. 307-322.

Michael Trupp

Michael Trupp

Michael Trupp  

The main developmental function of adolescence is defined as the establishment of a final sexual organization. Psychopathology of this period inevitably reflects some central abnormality of sexual development and function. Most vulnerable is the integration of bodily maturation and evolving self-representation. Conflicts of this type tend to be cumulative and should—according to the author—be viewed in a context specific to adolescence, i.e., not misconstrued by the perspectives of adult organization. Most dangerous is the adolescent's regressive surrender to proedipal, dependent asexuality. Some technical considerations of "laissez-faire" versus "role-playing" strategies of the analyst are discussed.

The author, a Jewish analyst practicing in Germany, notes the paradox of contemporary Germans' denunciation of their parents (and especially the parents' Nazi past) while they, the offspring, retain virulent anti-Semitic attitudes. The undoing of parental identification "in the ego" with coexistent retention of superego ideals is presented as explanatory. Possible broader applications of this mechanism throughout the sociological field are considered.

The Pietà series is viewed as "dreamlike pictorializations of the adult in contact with the primal phases of development." Oremland views the sculptural mergings and blurrings of the figures as both "inside" and "outside" of the artist, a variation of Winnicott's transitional space. Edited by Samuel A. Guttman, Randall L. Jones, and Stephen M. Parrish. Boston: G. K. Hall & Co., 1980. Vol. I, 1096 pp.; Vol. II, 916 pp.; Vol. III, 847 pp.; Vol. IV, 1130 pp.; Vol. V, 850 pp.; Vol. VI, 673 pp.

George Klumpner

George H. Klumpner
OAK PARK, ILL.

George Klumpner  

This Concordance will have considerable value for some users and some value for a considerable number of users. The purpose of this review is to help each reader to determine the value the Concordance may have for him or for her.

Concordances are designed to guide readers to particular words in their contexts. While a concordance itself sheds no new light on the text, it does, by assembling everything in the text containing any one word, provide a means for finding remembered passages and for comparing closely related passages. It is of particular value for linguistic research. Concordances can be used to locate a particular statement in a text, even if the user can only remember a single word in that statement. They can be used to compare and analyze word meanings, since some words have many different meanings, and they can be used to compare and analyze any changes the author has made in word usage over the years.

A concordance is a word index. Unlike a subject index, a word index guides the searcher to the words used by the author, but not necessarily to the subjects of the work. One strength of a concordance is that it is not selective: every occurrence of a word will be given in context, with no condensation. One strength of a subject index is that it does condense information that is related, so that the user can more quickly and easily find the listings for the information he or she seeks.

Concordances are now prepared with computers. Computers can be programmed to alphabetize, count, and segregate, but they cannot be programmed to think. Therein lie both the strengths and the weaknesses of all computer-generated concordances.

On Projection: A Study of Freud's Usage. Darius Ornston. Pp. 117-166.

Ornston presents an ambitious and scholarly tracing of Freud's use of projection as a conceptual continuum, as well as an examination of Freud's elaborators and critics on this subject. Certain borderline adolescent girls whose family lives have been unstable and whose fathers have been inconsistent are compared with Bess of Gershwin's Porgy and Bess. Their own sense of identity is diffuse, and they shift quickly from one man to another, alternately rebelling against and searching for the father-protector. Several case histories poignantly illustrate this pattern and emphasize the vital role of the therapist as stable, empathic transitional object, helping the patient toward conflict resolution and inner integration.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. XVII, 1978

The Effects of Caffeine and Methylphenidate on Hyperactive Children. Philip Firestone, et al. Pp. 445-456.

Twenty-one hyperactive children received in turn 500 mg. caffeine, 300 mg. caffeine, and 20 mg. methylphenidate per day in a double-blind cross-over design investigation. Each drug was given for three weeks. Methylphenidate resulted in significantly improved behavior in the children as rated by mothers and teachers and as indicated on tests of impulsivity and motor control. There were no significant improvements with either of the caffeine tests, although some children showed slight improvements with caffeine. The negative effects with both caffeine and methylphenidate were minimal.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. XVIII, 1979

Prediction of Child Maltreatment during Pregnancy. William A. Altmeier III, et al. Pp. 205-218.

Fourteen hundred expectant mothers volunteered to be interviewed about their attitudes, experiences, and knowledge of child rearing. The purpose of the interview was to identify parental predictors of child maltreatment. Based upon answers, two hundred seventy-three were expected to be at high risk for parenting disorders. After delivery, their infants and two hundred twenty-five selected randomly from all remaining mothers were followed in a double-blind fashion for evidence of child abuse, neglect, and nonorganic failure to thrive. All three parenting disorders were found significantly more often in the high-risk families.

Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. XVIII, 1979

An At-Risk Approach to the Study of Child Abuse. Some Preliminary Findings. Byron Egeland and Don Brunnquell. Pp. 219-235.

In an attempt to better understand the complex etiologies of child abuse and neglect, this investigation is following two hundred seventy-five high-risk mothers and infants through the child's first year of life. In the present study, the characteristics of a group of primiparous women, infant temperament, mother-infant interaction, and environmental stress factors are examined to identify variables that differentiate mothers who mistreat their children from those who do not. A subsample of twenty-five mothers providing good quality care and twenty-six mothers who have abused or in some way mistreated their children has been identified. The inadequate mothers had more pregnancy and birth complications, but there was little difference in the babies' temperament except that the babies in the good mother group were better able to orient and were less irritable. The good mothers were older, better educated, had more support from father and family, and, in general, were much better prepared for the baby. There was basically no difference in personality characteristics or amount of life stress experienced by the two groups of mothers. The variables that best differentiated the two groups were: mother's understanding of the psychological complexity of the infant and her relationship with the infant; and a factor based on observations of mother's caretaking skills, her positive affect, and the infant's social responsiveness.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Lawrence Sabot commented that Dr. Silverman's presentation was consistent with conclusions presented over the past decade in a growing body of studies in child development. Dr. Silverman indicated that there is a developmental line which culminates in adult feminine identity. Such a developmental line would preclude our considering the contributions and conflicts of any given libidinal phase as the sole significant determinant; instead, we would view the sense of femininity as an emerging entity, a confluence of self-representations, molded and shaped by external and internal influences along the developmental continuum. The small girl's reactions to the awareness of sexual differences are complicated by the almost unavoidable quota of narcissistic hurt experienced by all children during the rapprochement crisis. Dr. Sabot also questioned the curative effect of simply correcting early conceptual errors: the factors contributing to impaired self-esteem in a woman usually involve more than the misconceptions she had as a little girl. Stress must also be placed on the importance of identifications, of various ego and superego factors, and of the influence of family and culture. Dr. Barbara Deutsch remarked that the problem of the cognitive conceptualization of the female genitalia is compounded by the cloacal nature of bodily sensations in this area which increases the difficulty in discrimination. No matter how helpful and accurate parental information is, a little girl is unable to conceptualize this area accurately until the age of six or seven. A problem may remain for some women throughout adult life, even though they have cognitive capability. This is not so different from a child's incapacity to understand and conceptualize other mysteries, such as parental intercourse or where babies come from. For all little girls who have been observed, the discovery of the differences between the sexes brings narcissistic disappointment. Whether or not this becomes crucial in neurosis or in more severe pathological constructions depends on the matrix in which this narcissistic crisis occurs. In addition to the several factors Dr. Silverman mentioned, Dr. Deutsch would include innate factors and family trauma, such as the birth of siblings or the illness of a family member. Dr. Deutsch agreed with Dr. Silverman that interpretation of penis envy does not reach a bedrock beyond which no further analysis is required. Penis envy is most often a developmental metaphor whose important narcissistic underpinnings of difficulty with self-image and self-esteem must be analyzed.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Eleanor Galenson stated that considerable support for a genetic proposition such as Dr. Coleman offered for the "developmental phobia" comes from the data of infant observation. When a child is between 13 and 16 months of age, a number of ego functions, including intentionality, independent locomotion, and symbolic function, undergo definitive integration and stabilization. This involves a consolidation of the sense of self as distinct from the object, which appears to spark primary ambivalence. Hostile attacks on the mother are frequent at this age. Although the mother "in the flesh" is relatively safe from the effects of the attacks, the still unstable mental representation of the mother is not safe, and the parallel mental representation of the child as well as that of the mother must somehow be protected from the onslaughts of the child's primitive rage. The main thrust of development, then, seems to be the need to protect the object representation against the destructive force of the child's rage; the resulting regression and/or resomatization delays or inhibits the child's further individuation and ego development. Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

The Borderline Syndrome. Christa Rohde-Dachser. Pp. 481-527.

From a phenomenological perspective, borderline disturbances are situated on the boundaries between neuroses, psychoses, and the more serious character disturbances. In this paper the author attempts to delineate the syndrome, from a differential-diagnostic viewpoint, as an entity in itself. She integrates Kernberg's theory of the borderline personality organization with other theoretical approaches and with hypotheses of her own. According to Rohde-Dachser, the development of the borderline structure is initiated in the second to third year of life through a traumatization of the infantile striving for autonomy. This results in a specific pathology of the ego in which primitive splitting defenses predominate.

307

Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

The Necessity To Mourn. Margarete Mitscherlich-Nielsen. Pp. 981-990.

People in the Federal Republic of Germany live in the shadow of the repression and the denial of events which cannot be undone. The technique of screening out is expanding, and the incapacity for mourning results in a psychological immobilization; that is, in the inability to discover adequate, innovative solutions for the contemporary problems of our society in its international context. A self-image based on denial is easily damaged; criticism is intolerable. But the way to the future leads through the confrontation with the unmastered past.

Psyche. XXXIV, 1980

On the Way toward the Self: Comments on the Development of Psychoanalytic Theory of Recent Decades. Helmut Thomä. Pp. 221-245.

In the history of psychoanalysis, the theory of drives was the initial comprehensive interpretive framework. This was to be replaced first by the structural theory, then by ego psychology. Currently, theories of the self and of narcissism predominate. Thomä regards the tide of the "self" concept (which Freud used interchangeably with "ego" and "person") as a holistic reaction against the ego-psychological division of personal wholeness into functions. He points out that the "self," which has been presented as close to experience, is a theoretical construct and warns agains reifications in the theory of Kohut and his students.

Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

Observations on the Psychodynamics of an Intensive Care Unit. Rainer Schors. Pp. 343-363.

It is the task of an intensive care unit to eliminate death. The personnel of such a unit forms a "marginal group" at whose expense the members of society wish to spare themselves the confrontation with death, and this wish becomes an excessive demand upon the staff. Schors recounts the boundary rituals which

306

dominate life in intensive care units as well as the peculiar interactions with patients whose "careers" come to an end when they leave the unit—one way or another. He interprets these rituals and interactions as counterphobic acting out or, in the case of resuscitation, as discharge of aggression, and he recommends the introduction of group supervision.

Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

Experimental Rorschach Investigations of the "Pensée Opératoire." Rolf Vogt, et al. Pp. 829-873.

Clinical observations and metapsychological interpretations are almost inextricably mixed together in the concept of the pensée opératoire. The authors regard lack of imagination as the chief criterion of the pensée opératoire. They explain it on the basis of the psychoanalytic theory of fantasy and characterize it as a Rorschach fantasy syndrome. Comparing forty psychosomatic and forty psychoneurotic patients, they find that the former showed a lesser capacity for fantasy.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psyche. XXXIV, 1980

The Psychopathology of Patients with Myocardial Infarction. Emma Moersch, et al. Pp. 493-587.

Moersch summarizes theory in the field of psychosomatics. The question underlying the present investigation was: Under what psychological conditions, to be ascertained psychoanalytically, do patients suffer myocardial infarction? I. Kerz-Rühling reports on the available psychological literature concerning the genesis of heart disease and the structure of the cardiac patient's personality. S. Drews and R. D. Nern formulate the objectives and the execution of the study, which was concerned with the conceptualization not of psychological processes, but of the psychological conditions under which these arise. K. Kennel presents a case history—excerpts from an initial interview as well as comments. Structural conflicts which the patient acquired in childhood and which have become latent since then became mobilized in a life-historical crisis; the infarction appears as an answer to this crisis. R. Kelleter demonstrates that fixations on pregenital developmental stages are especially characteristic in this patient group. C. Rodriguez points out that object relations in an oral mode are typical. According to Kerz-Rühling, the specific defense constellation of myocardial infarction patients is the compensation for infantile deprivation by means of ideas of grandeur. These patients tend to deal with conflicts by denial; they usually decline psychotherapy of any duration. R. Fischer provides an overview of the contemporary theory of defense. The characteristic defense of these patients is to deny their dependence on others and their body perceptions. Compulsive defenses, repression, and projection are also observed.

310

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalytic Understanding of the Dream

By Paul Sloane, M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1979. 273 pp.

Donald Coleman

Donald Coleman

Donald J. Coleman
PITTSBURGH

Donald Coleman  

This book is a welcome addition to the list of books and monographs devoted to the psychoanalytic understanding of the dream. Following Freud, Sharpe, Fliess, the Kris Study Group, and Altman, the author has singled out the dream as an object of study. He approaches his subject from the vantage point of the supervisory session and the teaching seminar on dreams to illustrate technical aspects of teaching and of dream interpretation. The book is intended as a "handbook of the technique of dream analysis for psychoanalytic candidates" (p. 4). A sense of discovery, immediacy, and freshness to the work of understanding the dreamer is contributed by the classroom origin of this book. The disadvantages connected with this starting point become apparent to the reader as he/she proceeds through the many examples. Some readers will yearn for fewer examples and more analysis in depth, including a chance to follow the dreamer over time in the working through.

Because Freud's early work on jokes, slips, and dreams was written in a language foreign to candidates in the United States, the richness of detail and what linguists call the rhetoric or pragmatic aspects of the dream reporter's utterance has perhaps been lost to English-speaking readers. Lacan, for one, strongly reminds us of this possibility. With Sloane's particular interest in the manifest text and day residue, this richness is recovered.

114

Childhood and Folklore: A Psychoanalytic Study of Apache Personality

By L. Bryce Boyer, M.D. New York: The Library of Psychological Anthropology, 1979. 205 pp.

Joseph Lubart

Joseph Lubart

Joseph M. Lubart
NEW YORK

Joseph Lubart  

This book is a landmark effort in the application of psychoanalytic concepts to the study of culture. The author, through many years of intimate contact with the Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache Indians (including practicing psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy on their reservation in New Mexico), developed a deepening awareness of his patients and research subjects and of the folklore reflected in their education and rearing of children.

While knowledge existed from the early days of psychoanalysis that primary process thinking and conflicts, id drive derivatives, and tortuous use of ego defenses could be marked as similar in dreams and myths, seldom has there appeared as complete a treatment of the subject in a given culture as in this volume.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Broken Connection. On Death and the Continuity of Life

By Robert Jay Lifton. New York: Simon & Schuster, 1979. 495 pp.

Henry Krystal

Henry Krystal

Henry Krystal
SOUTHFIELD, MICH.

Henry Krystal  

Ever since his encounter with the survivors of Hiroshima, Lifton has devoted himself to explaining the themes of death and their impact upon life. Back in the early sixties, as we were preparing for his participation in our workshop on survivors of the Holocaust and on post-traumatic states, he told me that he intended to elaborate a "whole psychology" based upon "the encounter with death." This he has done. At the end of Death in Life1 he reiterated that in his opinion unlimited technological violence and absurd death have become more pressing for modern man than the Freudian focus on sexuality and moralism. In The Life of the Self2 he formulated the paradigms of death and the continuity of life as terms of a theory of symbolic immortality, evolving a death imagery, and applied it to psychopathology. Now, in The Broken Connection Lifton has proceeded to flesh out his conceptions of the effect of the encounter and consciousness of death upon the experience of living.

In the process of trying to work out some psychopathological conceptions, Lifton has surprised himself in returning to reconsider Freud's ideas, which he had dismissed lightly in earlier works. The deliberations of this book frequently revolve around a critique of Freud's and Erikson's psychopathological formulations. The result is that much of what he has to contribute from his journeys into the nether world can be quite compatible with the thinking of a modern American psychoanalyst.

Yeats. The Poetics of the Self

By David Lynch. Chicago and London: The University of Chicago Press, 1979. 240 pp.

Francis Baudry

Francis Baudry

Francis Baudry
NEW YORK

Francis Baudry  

David Lynch, a lecturer in English at Tufts, has written a thoughtful study on that extraordinary poet, William Butler Yeats. His work is on two levels—first, a detailed analysis of many poems organized as chapters dealing with themes of creativity and object relationships (Mistress or Muse, Fathers and Sons, Sons and Mothers, Fathers and Mothers). Each chapter presents a partial version of what Lynch argues is the narcissistic rather than the oedipal origin of Yeats's creativity.

The interpretation of the poem as texts of literature is woven into Yeats's personal language and his predilection for certain mythological themes and Irish historical figures.

The author presents a detailed précis of transitional phenomena in an attempt to explicate theoretical issues, definitions, and investigatory perspectives. He suggests that there is a clear division between transitional objects and transitional phenomena as well as between primary and secondary categories of objects. From this, a schedule and gradient matrix is derived, potentially capable of accommodating ethological and sociological observations—as well as more familiar developmental ones.

Evaluating the evolving transference status of the young child in analysis is extremely difficult. "Real" ongoing vicissitudes of home life and the "real" experience of the therapist by the patient—plus limitations of verbalization and abstract thought—have obscuring effects, both individually and in combination. The case of an impulse-ridden four-year-old boy with a history of severe maternal deprivation is used for illustration.

Adolescent Psychiatry. VI, 1978

Loneliness and the Adolescent. Eric Ostrov and Daniel Offer. Pp. 34-50.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

The experience of loneliness among a large number of teenage subjects is studied. Loneliness is defined as a painful inner craving for intimacy and closeness which, unlike depression, is characterized by hope. Adolescents are highly vulnerable to feelings of loneliness because of the push toward independence essential to their developmental stage. In their comparative survey of loneliness in over three thousand adolescents, the authors found the following statistically significant results: 1. Twelve- to fifteen-year-old boys and girls reported more loneliness than did sixteen- to twenty-year-olds. 2. Irish and Australian subjects (more stable societal rules?) reported less loneliness than their American counterparts. 3. Boys and girls who were in psychiatric hospitals and those in residential therapy for delinquency reported more loneliness than did normals. There was no significant difference between boys and girls of comparable ages.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

This is an extension of Gadpaille's major work in elucidating the formation of healthy psychosexual identity in children and adolescents. He concludes, through much cross-cultural research (with reference to nonhuman mammalian studies as well), that the various stages of sexual identity (i.e., gender identity, sex-role consolidation, sexual choice, comfort with genital sexuality) have relatively fixed, innate critical periods for development. Adolescents in our society have much discomfort with, fear of, and guilt about their sexuality. This constitutes a lack of "heterosexual readiness," caused by enormous prohibition during the critical period of children's curiosity and exploration of their own bodies and those of children of the opposite sex. There is "a remarkable infrequency of either sexual deviations or sexual dysfunctions in cultures permissive of childhood sex play and curiosity.

Adolescent Psychiatry. VI, 1978

The Borderline Aspects of Adolesecence and the Borderline State. Peter L. Giovacchini. Pp. 320-338.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

Giovacchini believes that in the literature too much emphasis is placed upon description and definition of the borderline conditions and too little upon improving and understanding therapeutic interactions. The term "borderline," he feels, is used to describe very heterogeneous conditions which have in common: 1) structural defects, and 2) early developmental fixations resulting in a "primitive" mental state. He postulates an analogy between the borderline states and adolescence. In both there is an identity diffusion, a diffuseness of the inner self-representation. He views borderline states as pathological exaggerations of the borderline qualities of adolescence. He illustrates his hypothesis with the case history of a borderline adolescent, currently in treatment. The case demonstrates the difficulty of establishing a "therapeutic foothold" with borderline patients, as well as the common feeling of inadequacy engendered in the therapist by such patients who "use" their ego defects as defenses to control and manipulate.

143

The author, after defining her concept of borderline as congruent with the concepts of Kernberg and Masterson, outlines her treatment and adult follow-up of seven borderline adolescent outpatients. Although some patients in early adulthood show evidence of better object relations than others, all are still functioning in the borderline range. They have, however, with the aid of therapy, apparently been able to do some "catching up" in the direction of improved ego integration.

Meetings of the New York Psychoanalytic Society

September 25, 1979. RECONSTRUCTION OF AN ACCIDENT EXPERIENCED DURING THE RAPPROCHEMENT SUBPHASE: INNOVATIONS IN RESPONSE TO PHASE-SPECIFIC ARREST. Dr. Muriel Chaves Winestine.

During the first two years of analytic therapy with a motorically precocious boy, Dr. Winestine reconstructed an accident (falling backward down a steep flight of stairs) that had occurred in the child's twenty-first month of life. The reconstruction permitted Dr. Winestine to apply Dr. Mahler's observations on the rapprochement subphase to the understanding of this young patient. The discrepancy between the infant's physical precocity and his phase-specific emotional dependence on his mother, as well as the accident itself, interfered with the successful negotiation of his anal phase. What resulted, according to Dr. Winestine, included a faulty neutralization of aggression, a paucity of imaginative play, and a failure to successfully master the precocious (and therefore discrepant) motor development which, in turn, were responsible for faulty structural development. This led Dr. Winestine to make innovations in treatment technique which aimed at a better resolution of the dyadic, independence-dependence conflict epitomized in the rapprochement crisis.

The boy was referred for treatment by the staff of his kindergarten at the age of five years and four months because of an inability to adapt to his surroundings. He was isolated and preoccupied with issues of cleanliness and messiness. He refused to participate in planned and group activities, drank and urinated with inordinate frequency, and was not affectionate with his teachers. The parents (recently separated), after being alerted to watch for symptoms at home, reported the following: increased physical and emotional constraint, fear of noises, sleeplessness, and withdrawal to bed with complaints of stomachaches when upset. He also spent a great deal of time by himself reading and writing numbers and letters, and this seemed a corollary to his earlier refusal to have stories read to him. He had walked unaided at eight and a half months of age. After his traumatic fall, he was unhurt, but quite dazed; physical examination at the time showed no injury.

[[RunningHead]]

Freud and his Patients. Volume II of the Downstate Psychoanalytic Institute's Twenty-Fifth Anniversary Series

Edited by Mark Kanzer, M.D., and Jules Glenn, M.D. New York/London: Jason Aronson, 1980. 452 pp.

Harry Trosman

Harry Trosman

Harry Trosman
CHICAGO

Harry Trosman  

This book, one of a series of four, is published in commemoration of the twenty-fifth anniversary of The Psychoanalytic Institute at New York University, which until 1979 was the Downstate Psychoanalytic Institute. This second volume of the series consists of twenty-eight papers written by members of the Institute and concerned with Freud's major case histories. There are five papers on Dora, three on Little Hans, seven on the Rat Man, six on Schreber, and six on the Wolf Man. Each case includes an integrative summary. There is an introductory chapter by Jules Glenn on pertinent psychoanalytic concepts as they are relevant to the cases and to Freud's countertransference. There is also a closing chapter by Mark Kanzer, summarizing the various papers.

Although occasional references are made to patients other than the subjects of the five major case histories (Katharina of Studies on Hysteria and the "homosexual woman of 1920" are referred to by Glenn in a paper on Freud's adolescent patients), the collectivity of Freud's patients is not the subject of this monograph. Nor does the book deal with the growing body of literature written by some of Freud's patients—Wortis, Kardiner, Grinker, etc.—which describes their treatment from the patient's point of view. Rather, the authors have largely confined their studies to what have come to be called the pillars upon which the psychoanalytic structure rests. Of the five major case reports, one concerned a child whom Freud did not directly treat, another concerned a psychotic man whom Freud never saw. Thus, in the strictest sense the book is about Freud, three psychoanalytic patients, and two others.

This narrowing of the view, however, takes nothing away from the usefulness of the book. By concentrating on the published case reports, the authors continue a tradition well established in psychoanalytic education.

260

American Psychoanalysis: Origins and Development. The Adolf Meyer Seminars

Edited by Jacques Quen and Eric T. Carlson. New York: Brunner/Mazel, 1978. 216 pp.

Lewis Robbins

Lewis Robbins

Lewis L. Robbins
GLEN OAKS, N.Y.

Lewis Robbins  

This publication of the Adolf Meyer Seminars, which were given at Cornell Medical Center, provides an accurate historical perspective while also presenting discussions of the current status of psychoanalysis and its future. The series goes significantly beyond previously available material and "sets the record straight" about a number of controversial issues that arose over the years. Many of

262

these issues, involving matters of theory and training, were colored by the personalities of some of the early leaders. Each of the speakers is eminently qualified to discuss his or her particular topic and does so in a most literate fashion.

Although Freud did not view the United States as the optimum soil for the growth of psychoanalysis, the circumstances of history shifted the locus of its developmental struggles and successes to these shores. The first three chapters deal with the European origins of and reactions to psychoanalysis, the American response to it, and the impact psychoanalysis has had on our culture. Psychoanalysis as a psychological system incorporates a body of ideas for which the times were ripe at the beginning of the twentieth century, both in Europe and in the United States. Great changes in all the arts reflected an awareness of unconscious mental processes and a desire to express deeper emotions. Interest in and attitudes about sexuality were being openly discussed, and sexual mores were freer than they had been in the earlier Victorian period. Medicine was strongly organic in its orientation and resisted any psycho-etiological theories of illness, the Cartesian mind-body dualism was firmly held, and there was considerable reluctance to accept Freud's monistic view of mental health and illness.

In America "nurture over nature" was stressed more than it was in Europe, which led to a greater optimism regarding the changeability of human psychology and the treatability of mental illness. Psychoanalysis was viewed as the best method by which successful treatment might be accomplished.

Explorations in Psychoanalysis

By Ralph R. Greenson, M.D. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1978. 578 pp.

Wayne Myers

Wayne Myers

Wayne A. Myers
NEW YORK

Wayne Myers  

The late Ralph R. Greenson's book presents a collection of thirty-two of his clinical and technical papers on psychoanalysis. In the preface to the book, the author informs us that the papers will tell us something about himself, as well as about his patients. This contention is well borne out in the text that follows.

My major thesis in this review is that many of the articles in this collection give evidence that Greenson, throughout his career, was in considerable conflict with a crucial aspect of psychoanalytic theory and technique—the centrality of the transference in the understanding and resolution of neurosis. By emphasizing the working alliance and the so-called "real" aspects of the relationship between patient and analyst in so many of his papers, Greenson, it seems to me, was attempting to dethrone transference interpretation as the royal (perhaps even the sole) road along which analyst and patient must travel in their attempt to work through the material in an analysis. He consistently advocates, as a replacement for the classical technical approach, the analyst's allowing his own "real" persona to shine through to the patient.

One of Greenson's early papers, "The Mother Tongue and the Mother" (1950), illustrates my thesis. In this work, the author contends that his young female patient was enabled to break through to the important affects bound up in the early mother-child interaction only by virtue of his suggestion that the analysis be switched from her adopted language, English, to her mother tongue, German.

Themes of Work and Love in Adulthood

Edited by Neil J. Smelser and Erik H. Erikson. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1980. 297 pp.

Leon Altman

Leon Altman

Leon L. Altman
NEW YORK

Leon Altman  

In May, 1977, a group of sociologists and behavioral scientists, including some, such as Smelser and Erikson, trained in psycho-analysis, met at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences in Palo Alto, California, for "unstructured exploratory discussion" on the "human life-cycle as a whole, focusing especially on the developmental vicissitudes of the adult years." It would appear that there is "a burgeoning interest in life-stage theory," as one of the contributors (M. Fiske, p. 243) points out, and this is reflected in the nature and content of the book.

The conference was deliberately interdisciplinary; the book is equally so, although the sociocultural approach assumes a dominant position. The interdisciplinary idea is certainly commendable, but when a series of essays of this nature is bound between the covers of a book, the volume should be carefully edited so that the jargon of one discipline does not bcome another discipline's stumbling block.

The title of the book notwithstanding, work plays a minor role, and love has merely a walk-on part. And if the thematic unity suggested by the title is not maintained, the reason may lie in the fact that the real intent of the book is to "identify central issues" that have come to dominate the study of adulthood as a developmental phase in its own right.

A considerable proportion of the contributions conveys the impression that the data base consisted of responses to questions and questionnaires. Yet, several of the contributors, especially J. Giele, confirm that data so obtained is not reliable and can lead to conflicting conclusions. There appears to be no unitary theory, as yet, on the nature of development during adulthood. The prevailing intellectual atmosphere conveyed by this book is of subjective impressions, broad generalizations, and rather tentative conclusions based on sociological research methods.

Countertransference and Seduction. Julien Rouart. Pp. 413-442.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Rouart reviews the narrow and broad definitions of countertransference, including in his study the recent work of Michel Neyraut in France and of Kohut in the United States. Both these authors have widened our understanding of the phenomena of empathy and countertransference. Even though Kohut does not pose the question explicitly, his work is of great importance to the problems of countertransference, the development of empathy, and the capacity to be an analyst. Narcissistic transference phenomena enter into any analysis at some time or other. The analyst's capacity for empathy derives, according to Kohut, from early but tolerable traumatization at the primitive phases in development. The outcome of such traumatization is the development of an extreme perceptual sensitivity, together with the secondary process modalities for the understanding and organization of such psychological stimuli. Seduction, which is earlier in origin and wider in scope than generally supposed, is involved in this traumatization in narcissism and in countertransference. It is one of the earliest manifestations of communication and is characteristic of the earliest moments of life in the original relationship with the mother. Hence the concepts of trauma and seduction aid in understanding transference and countertransference phenomena. The analytic situation is, in effect, a technically provoked traumatic situation, permitting the reappearance of past situations of danger, but with the energic discharge in small, discontinuous, and controlled doses.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XL, 1976

Countertransferences. Jean Guillaumin. Pp. 455-482.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

In Guillaumin's view, countertransference originates in the transference of the patient in the analytic situation. He would include in this not only the transference of the patient, but the former transferences of the analyst to his own analyst as well as to other important individuals in his life. The analyst may, in fact, discharge his own earlier transferences in the analytic setting while maintaining his professional identity by relying on the countertransference of his own analyst. There are countertransferences of filiation, borrowing, and inheritance, which confront us with the narcissism of the analyst through his defensive idealization of his analyst-parent. The seductive aspects of the countertransference bring into play archaic and pregenital aspects of the analyst's personality. Yet only the analyst with a need to be all-powerful and a need to feel always secure against passive moments would attempt to deny these seductive aspects. Finally, the task of the analyst is to manage the countertransference in such a manner as to maintain a tolerance for the fantasies which develop in the transitional space of treatment. This would involve ultimately maintaining at the same time the anaclitic and transitional relationship upon which treatment depends while also maintaining the goal of analyzing the oedipal conflicts of the patient. The analyst, then, is called upon to be at the same time a maternal, nurturing object and an oedipal object in the transference.

298

Balkányi claims that language develops as a restitution for loss of pleasure in touching and feeling the concrete reality of mother's body. This sensual cathexis of the representation of things is more or less abandoned for the advantage that accrues with the investment in word representations. Yet many linguists refuse to collaborate with analysts, and analysts sometimes think that their work has nothing to do with linguistic science. This sterile state of isolation is compounded by the technical languages of the two disciplines.

The Cathexis of Meaning. Michèlle Perron-Borelli. Pp. 681-692.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

The author discusses her child's acquisition of language. A journey and separation were involved. She concludes that meaning was cathected in the crucial experiences of communication between mother and child and that this cathexis had the double aim of narcissistic restoration and conservation of the object. The first meaningful utterances are personal creations of the child which are recognized and invested in return by the mother. Meaning in this instance was at first the naming of a class of objects which were simultaneously maternal substitutes and identificatory supports. The cathexis of meaning also opened the way for the cathexis of reality. Meaning permitted an escape from the solipsistic enclosure and was an attempt to control the trauma of loss and separation. Concomitantly it permits the breakup of the dyadic relationship, facilitating displacement onto new objects.

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLI, 1977

The Sense of Despair. The Problem of Depression in Psychoanalytic Theory. A. Haynal. Pp. 17-186.

This is a detailed summary of the psychoanalytic literature on depression and the depressive affect. The review ranges over childhood developmental studies, discussions of helplessness, loss, grief, boredom, and the function of mourning in the analytic process and in creativity. Haynal attempts to integrate the various viewpoints; the schools of psychoanalytic thought are only apparently divergent concerning depression. Their different languages stem not so much from different viewpoints but from the complexity of dynamic, economic, and topographical (structural) factors involved in the depressive affect. Haynal focuses on depressive affect as experienced in, among other places, the course of psychoanalytic treatment. Abraham had already complained of the role assigned to the depressive affect as a poor relation taking second place to anxiety. This role was assigned from the beginning by Freud, himself a depressive whose self-analysis was initiated in the course of mourning for his father. Depression seemed to be studied more by the Kleinian school or by others on the margin of or clearly outside the Freudian group. Nonetheless, many analysts, especially the Budapest group (Bak, Balint, Benedek, Gero, Harnik, Rado) became interested in the relation to the primary object and touched on the theme of depression more fully. For Haynal, the capital moment in the evolution of the human being is the universal experience of the progressive loss of the mother. From this experience the depressive affect develops. It is thus concomitant with the loss of omnipotence and fusion during separation-individuation. Depression occurs at the moment of passing from a narcissistic to an object-related organization. This passage involves an all-important experience of helplessness (Hilflosigkeit) and the abandonment of feelings of omnipotence. Out of the loss comes the desire to substitute something for what was lost. This principle of functioning of the psychic apparatus is linked, in a sense, with the principle of constancy. The restoration of the lost object is thus a part of human nature. In the second part of his report, Haynal gives an extensive historical study of the evolution of psychoanalytic theories about depression. In this section, however, he concentrates on authors somewhat difficult of access to the French-speaking analysts he addressed at the Congress. There are included, however, good discussions of such contemporary French theorists as Lebovici, Mallet, Nacht and Racamier, Pasche, Grunberger, and Bergeret.

Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

The Critique of Objectivism in Psychology. Walter Herzog. Pp. 289-305.

In order to attain scientific standing, psychology has chosen classical physics as its methodological ideal. The primacy of method, appropriated without regard to its specific objectives, entailed the elevation of whatever is physically measurable to the status of "true" reality. Thus, psychology lost its "object," namely the experiencing subject whose perception and behavior are laden with meaning. Psychology's critique of psychoanalysis continues to judge the latter by the external criteria of scientism, overlooking its specific accomplishment—the formulation of a new method of inquiry which is appropriate to its object.

Patients at a university outpatient clinic who suffered from impotence or premature ejaculation and who met certain selection criteria were referred for psychoanalytically oriented short-term psychotherapy with a maximum of twenty-four sessions. Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

Are There Two Psychoanalytic Techniques? Johannes Cremerius. Pp. 577-599.

There are two contrasting treatment techniques which co-exist within the contemporary framework of psychoanalysis—classical insight therapy (or the intervention of paternal reason) and therapy as corrective emotional experience—derived respectively from Freud and Ferenczi. Whereas the "classical" therapy presupposes the patient's oedipal attainments and addresses itself therapeutically to conflict, the "maternal" holding therapy is oriented toward preoedipal stages of development and addresses itself therapeutically to defects. The author believes that technical innovations grow out of theoretical reinterpretation and poses the question of whether either technique can dispense with the other.

Psychoanalytic Experiences in the Supervision of Pregnancy Counseling. Klaus Menne and Emma Moersch. Pp. 121-151.

During the years 1976 and 1977, one hundred twenty cases were presented and discussed in the context of psychoanalytic supervision at the Pro Familia center in Frankfurt. Behind inadequate contraceptive practices of the pregnant women who wish to terminate their pregnancies and long delays before applying to the counseling center, one can discover conflicts with their partners and intrapsychic conflicts between the unconscious wish for a child and oedipal guilt feelings. The imposed advice deprives the pregnant woman of the opportunity to realize her own ambivalence and to make a decision on her own. Instead she is obliged to delegate the resolution of her conflict to an external (superego) agency which may ally itself with her unconscious wish against the ego.

Grimm's fairy tales may be read as a prescientific psychology of development. The authors propose the hypothesis that sociocultural background, symptoms, and medical terminology undergo historical changes, but that the structure and dynamics of psychic disturbances are neutral vis-à-vis such change and remain essentially identical. Herbert F. Waldhorn—1919-1981

Charles Brenner

Charles Brenner

Charles Brenner  

While this issue of the Quarterly was in press, news came of the death of one of our editors, Dr. Herbert F. Waldhorn. He died suddenly on 16 June 1981 of a cardiac arrest due to the chronic arterial disease which had cast a shadow over his life and had forced him to limit his activity progressively for a dozen years before his untimely death.

Dr. Waldhorn was a New Yorker born and bred. He attended Columbia College and New York University Medical School, from which he graduated in 1942. He was on active military duty as a psychiatrist from 1943 to 1946, serving first in the army and later in the Office of Strategic Services. For him, as for many of his contemporaries, discharge from the army was the beginning of his career as a psychoanalyst. He enrolled in the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, from which he was graduated in 1952 and where he later became a training and supervising analyst. From 1961 to 1963 he was secretary of the New York Psychoanalytic Society. He served on many committees of both Society and Institute during his professional career, notably as a director of the Society and as an editor of the Monograph Series of the Ernst Kris Study Group of the Institute. In addition, he was active in the affairs of the American Psychoanalytic Association, where he served on the Program Committee for several years and as secretary of the Association from 1965 to 1968. For a number of years before his death he was actively involved in the resident training program of the Hillside Hospital. In 1975 he joined the Editorial Board of the Quarterly, becoming its book review editor in 1979.

Dr. Waldhorn published several articles in the field of psychoanalysis as well as many summaries, reviews, panel reports, and critiques. Notable among them are a paper on assessment of analyzability, which appeared in Volume 29 of the Quarterly,

[[RunningHead]]

Fantasy and Symbol. Studies in Anthropological Interpretation. Essays in Honour of George Devereux

Edited by R. H. Hook. London/New York: Academic Press, Inc., 1979. 304 pp.

Werner Muensterberger

Werner Muensterberger

Werner Muensterberger
LONDON

Werner Muensterberger  

Festschriften have become a laudable tradition as a well-deserved expression of professional standing and esteem. They represent a commendable way by which colleagues and students honor the accomplishments of a scholar or scientist. Such a collection of essays reminds one of a birthday party when well-wishing guests bring presents which they deem appropriate. The presents vary and are of necessity hardly alike in terms of scope and concern. Fantasy and Symbol marks George Devereux's seventieth birthday, and the volume contains a number of contributions which are meant to give evidence of the special regard in which Devereux's manifold writings on various aspects of anthropology and psychoanalysis are held. "To render George Devereux homage to his measure," writes Claude Lévi-Strauss, "one would have to prove oneself at once ethnologist, Hellenist and psychoanalyst," while Professor Weston LaBarre, with transparent affection, speaks of the honored recipient of these learned papers as the "universally acknowledged … ranking world authority in psychoanalytic anthropology." No wonder that well-known as well as young and aspiring scholars use the occasion to express their homage in a variety of contributions which reflect the cast of Devereux's impressive mind.

Besides R. H. Hook's introductory overview and his discussion of the main theme of this volume, namely, fantasy and symbol from a psychoanalytic angle, there is a biographical account by Ariane Deluz of Devereux's life and work. The book actually opens with a contribution to his Festschrift by George Devereux himself. His paper, "Fantasy and Symbol as Dimensions of Reality," underlines a theorem he has elaborated in many aspects: that in anthropological perspective "the guarantor of fantasy is reality" while from the psychoanalytic point of view "the guarantor of reality is fantasy," which in a way is the keynote of this collection of articles.

We find allusions to this issue in several of the essays.

Das Borderline-Syndrom. (The Borderline Syndrome.)

By Christa Rohde-Dachser. Bern/Stuttgart/Vienna: Verlag Hans Huber, 1979. 247 pp.

Rudolf Ekstein

Rudolf Ekstein

Rudolf Ekstein
LOS ANGELES

Rudolf Ekstein  

It is impressive to note the degree to which the author of this work is familiar with and influenced by the thinking of American psychiatric and psychoanlaytic authors. She is deeply influenced by the recent contributions of Kernberg and Kohut, whose explanations of narcissistic states are said to help define limits and provide clearer definitions for the notion of the borderline. She discusses the theories of Kernberg, Mahler, Searles, and Wolberg to make the point that the borderline syndrome is a specific developmental disturbance which characterizes the processes of separation and individuation.

Rohde-Dachser attempts a synthesis and an explanation of the various clinical manifestations of the borderline patient. She sees the borderline syndrome as a special strategy for the solution of conflicts in the area of ego development, genetically derived from processes of separation and individuation in which pathologically created points of fixation and certain repressions of the ego come to be manifested as the borderline phenomena. Essentially she sees the borderline syndrome as one of the sequelae of the renouncing of autonomy.

A particularly valuable aspect of the book is the author's regularly combining an explanation of an aspect of the structure of the borderline personality with a consideration of the way in which the ideas being focused on are reflected in the attitude taken by the therapist in his attempt to help the patient. For example, discussing the concept of ego deficit or ego weakness, she suggests that those who use this concept could easily fall into an attitude of therapeutic nihilism and assume that borderline patients are psychic cripples who cannot really be helped. Preferring to think of ego deficit in terms of the functions served by such a deficit, she then speaks of such ego weakness as a defensive operation which undermines cognitive functions, functions of perception, etc.

[[RunningHead]]

Cyprus—War and Adaptation. A Psychoanalytic History of Two Ethnic Groups in Conflict

By Vamik D. Volkan, M.D. Charlottesville: University of Virginia Press, 1979. 192 pp.

Martin Wangh

Martin Wangh

Martin Wangh
JERUSALEM

Martin Wangh  

Vamik D. Volkan's book is bound to be of interest to those analysts who are intrigued by problems of the emigrant-immigrant analyst who has passed from one cultural environment to another, and to those who seek ways by which psychoanalysis can make a contribution

436

to the understanding of history or of the evolution of social events in general.

Volkan suggests that the chief source of the bloody conflict between the Greeks and the Turks on the island of Cyprus is the fear of merging, of losing identity, and that underneath this fear lies a strong, regressive tendency toward a return to a symbiotic relationship with a clan's powerful mother. According to the author, the maternal figure is powerful among Greeks and Turks alike, despite the fact that externally these family clans are organized along strongly paternal, authoritarian lines. The persistent need for distancing oneself from such a central mother figure is met in major ways by defensive "splitting." (Kernberg's discussion of the borderline and narcissistic personality is Volkan's main guide in viewing ethnic matters in this way.) The existing "bipolarity" of Greeks and Turks lends itself to and is fostered for purposes of "externalization." By displacing the central conflict with the mother from the intrafamilial to the interethnic arena, the members of the groups achieve and maintain repression. The displacement is entirely ego-syntonic because from early on1 the Turkish mother, having been brought up in the same way, feeds prejudice against the Greek. She transmits to her baby the feeling that a visting Greek is a guest to be feared.

Because Greek and Turkish clans resemble each other so closely in structure and behavior, Volkan thinks they see each other as mutual mirror images (he must mean "unconsciously," although he does not make this explicit). Out of fear of merging, i.e., remerging with the externalized parts of the self, they must keep a distance from one another.

These arguments are introduced in connection with portions of Volkan's self-analysis which are thought to bear on the issues under examination. It is clear that Volkan has pursued directions and depths through his self-analysis which his official analysis did not reach. What are the dilemmas of one who has left his native land (Cyprus) and has stopped using his native tongue (Turkish)?

This article, as its author himself indicates, raises more questions than it answers. The discussion by John Demos is perhaps more illuminating in

450

regard to studies in psychoanalytic history than is the article itself. However, the article is useful in that it points up the real difficulties involved in psychohistory. The most important statement is Demos's comment that we need "a new and different theory, a theory of group psychology, no more and no less, in order to cross this next frontier of psychohistory." It seems that we have not gone very far in formulating a real scientific methodological approach to psychohistory.

Psychoanalytic Aspects of Religious Experience. W. W. Meissner. Pp. 103-141.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The author elaborates on the psychoanalytic aspects of religious experience. His arguments are introduced by a consideration of various historical polarities, such as consciousness versus unconsciousness; freedom versus determinism; the teleological versus the causal, the epigenetic versus the reductionistic; the moral versus the instinctual; and finally the supernatural versus the natural. In all of these he attempts to reconcile psychoanalytic concepts with some form of religious belief. The only one in which he feels that they are quite irreconcilable is the last one, the supernatural versus the natural. Then, in great detail and in scholarly fashion, he discusses what he considers to be various errors in Freud's theory of religious experience, although none too convincingly. The next large section of his article, titled "Developmental Schema," is divided into three major areas: 1) narcissism; 2) dependence; and 3) faith. His discussions of the first two are quite clear and provide interesting reviews; in the third, however, the schema he develops is somewhat difficult to follow.

Gehrie feels that psychoanalytic theory can become more useful through the understanding of anthropology, and in this article he seeks to bridge the gap between the two. In discussing the interface between these two areas of investigation, he cites a number of factors. One which has been neglected in the past pertains to the distinctions between fantasy and reality and between conscious and unconscious knowledge. Two other phenomena which may connect the two disciplines are empathy and countertransference. Perhaps the most cogent observation made in the article is the following: "We are, it seems, in the painful but promising stage of being forced to accommodate our method to our data, rather than taking the reverse route…" Although there has been progress in bringing these two fields together, there are still many obstacles to such a synthesis.

Self Representation and the Capacity for Self Care. Henry Krystal. Pp. 209-246.

James Bing

James Bing

James Bing  

The author summarizes this rather complicated and somewhat repetitious paper fairly well when he states that drug dependent and psychosomatic patients suffer from: 1) a marked disturbance of affect development, and 2) and inability to exercise self-caring functions. Krystal traces these difficulties back to complicated situations during the early developmental period in which the defect is in the mothering process, or at least in the fantasies the developing individual has in respect to the care-taking object. The difficulties in treating such patients result primarily from the fact that they are unable to confront their own aggression without becoming either severely depressed or homicidal, particularly in reference to the therapist. But in a few selected instances, according to the author, intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy has been able to produce dramatic results, although it demands an enormous amount of patience, tolerance, and empathy on the part of the therapist. Perhaps one of the most stimulating thoughts expressed in this paper is that an individual can no more affect his autonomically controlled organs than one can influence one's organs that are affected by "hysterical paralysis." Such a concept has far-reaching implications.

453

From a rather short period of observing two children, five and six years of age, Baum generalizes about the origins of creativity. Each of the children had had early significant parental and object losses. The author feels that their creative manifestations are evidence of the need to master narcissistic conflict. While the article is interesting, these children were not in analysis and thus the material is relatively superficial. The author's conclusions on the basis of the patients' histories are highly speculative.

Dorpat describes three patients who had accidents repeatedly because "for them, omnipotence and invulnerability resided in the idealized self object." Assuming the author's dynamic analysis of the production of these accidents is correct, several aspects of his approach might nevertheless be questioned. For instance, he differentiates these "accidents" from action; also, he describes these "accidents" as though they are unrelated to psychic factors. The usefulness of the article lies in its reminding us that the psychodynamics of repeated accidents is often overlooked.

Barratt and Schafer are in agreement in one area, namely, that psychoanalysis has to be separated from natural science. But the author feels that Schafer's attempt to validate this imperative by means of "a new language for psychoanalysis" is erroneous and serves no useful purpose. He shows how Schafer's ideas are an outgrowth of Wittgensteinian philosophy, with a little of Ryle and Sartre added. Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic. XLIII, 1979

The Sensory Deprivations. An Approach to the Study of the Emergence of Affects and the Capacity for Object Relations. David A. Freedman. Pp. 29-68.

S. Seides

S. Seides

S. Seides  

Three modes of sensory deprivation are explored with respect to their associations with specific and predictable psychological vulnerabilities. These are congenital blindness, congenital deafness, and severe environmental deprival during the first three years of life. While twenty-five percent of congenitally blind infants become autistic, autism in the congenitally deaf appears to be no greater than it is in the general population. Six months seems to be the age by which the parents of congenitally blind children seek consultation for their child's deviant behavior, while parents of congenitally deaf children may wait until they are about three years old. Such observations offer persuasive evidence that during the early development of normal children there is a shift in the sensory modality through which the child perceives and organizes experience. The relation with the mother seems to be critical in organizing and channeling aggression. In the environmentally deprived, absence of contact with the mother limits the basic internalizations which allow for a differentiation of self and nonself. Affect as a subjective event and affective expression are not the same. Affective expression is the more primitive in the maturational time-table and leads to synthesis of the two. Thus, Freedman suggests extending Hartmann's concept of an undifferentiated phase to include all elements of psychological functioning: affects, drives, object relations, and structures. Maturation proceeds according to a gene-determined timetable, but how developmental potentials emerge is a function of the psychological ambience in which they occur, i.e., developmental factors.

In an attempt to clarify the nature of the unintelligibility of analysands' communications during analysis, the author discusses the problem from the viewpoints of linguistics, cognitive activities, and historical reconstructions. He rejects Lacan's postulate that neurosis is caused by the unintelligibility arising from the use of abstract language. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry. VIII, 1979

The Concept of Death and Suicidal Behavior in Young Children. Three Case Studies. Israel Orbach and Hananyah Glaubman. Pp. 668-678.

Case studies are reported of two girls who attempted suicide and one boy who threatened to commit suicide. The analysis of their interviews substantiates the hypothesis that a unique cognitive conceptualization of death plays a role in the suicidal behavior of children. The children of these studies regarded themselves as being able to undergo "life-like" experiences after death. They had two conceptions about death: impersonal death, referring to other people; and personal death, referring to their own death. The latter was regarded as another form of life and as reversible. Theoretical and clinical implications concerning children's suicidal behavior are suggested.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

The State of Research on Ego Identity: A Review and Appraisal. Part II. Edmund Bourne. Pp. 371-392.

In the first part of this review a comprehensive survey of empirical research on ego identity was presented. Special emphasis was given to the large number of studies employing James Marcia's "identity status" paradigm. Research within this paradigm is recapitulated here by presenting empirical results which typify each of the four identity statuses (i.e., achievement, moratorium, foreclosure, and diffusion). A detailed evaluation of the identity status paradigm itself follows. Among the topics considered are (1) the construct and external validity of the approach as a whole, (2) the rationale and discriminant validity of the identity statuses, and (3) the reliability of the Identity Status Interview. Part II concludes by considering a number of problems for future research. Several persisting methodological and substantive issues within the identity status paradigm are noted. Finally, it is suggested that investigators turn their attention to the processes mediating identity formation. Contemporary psychoanalytic conceptions of adolescent development are viewed as providing one possible theoretical framework for investigating such processes.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VII, 1978

Family Interaction Patterns among Families with Normal, Disturbed, and Drug-Abusing Adolescents. Carol A. Gantman. Pp. 429-440.

The relationship between family interaction patterns and the symptomatology of the individual family member are central to many therapeutic approaches. This study was designed to determine whether family interaction patterns differ significantly among three groups of families defined according to the adolescent offspring's symptoms. Thirty families were evaluated in a one-hour interview while three observers behind a one-way mirror rated verbal behavior and the quality of interaction between father, mother, and adolescent. Assessed behaviors included the ability to reach a decision, decision time, scapegoating, and doublebind messages. In addition, the quality of the family's interaction was assessed at four different times during the interview. The results established that the three family groups did not differ demographically. A comparison of the two disturbed family groups yielded no significant differences, with the exception of the adolescent's presenting problem and behaviors. The normal group was significantly different from the other two groups in frequency of scapegoating of the adolescent and the ability to reach a decision. Additionally, the normal families displayed clearer communications, more freedom of expression, more cooperation, and greater sensitivity among members. Several variables did not discriminate the normal group from the disturbed family groups.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VIII, 1979

Drug and Alcohol Use, Delinquency, and Vandalism Among Upper Middle Class Pre-and Post-Adolescents. Edward M. Levine and Conrad Kozak. Pp. 91-101.

This article analyzes data from a survey research study of students in the fifth through twelfth grades of an upper middle-class Chicago suburban community. The findings indicate the use of alcohol and drugs among both prepubertal and teenage students and the involvement of both groups in theft and vandalism. The level of community affluence and quality of community institutions and services rule out the explanations usually offered in studies of delinquency in lower class and low-income communities. Peer group pressures and psychogenic factors appear to influence these kinds of acting-out behavior. And since considerable numbers of students noted that their parents had not established certain important regulations for them, the view advanced by this study is that deficient socialization and inadequate parenting also appear to be causes of these behavioral problems. However, since the study did not categorize the data in a way to permit cross-tabulations either supporting or invalidating this argument, this conclusion is a tentative one. It is suggested that future research dealing with these problems in this social stratum investigate the influence of parenting on acting-out behavior.

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

January 7, 1980. ON SOME EARLY COMPONENTS OF THE SPLIT PARENTAL IMAGO IN ANALYSIS, IN MYTH, AND IN RELIGION. Renato J. Almansi, M.D.

Dr. Almansi presented data from clinical analyses and from his study of myth and religious symbolism, in order to shed light on some of the earliest perceptual experiences which contribute to the formation of the object and to the split parental imago. Citing Mahler, Kernberg, and Blos, he stated that this imago is born in the early contacts between mother and child. The primitive perceptual experiences arising from these early contacts provide the raw material from which part objects and symbolization emerge. In every analysis an effort is made to reconstruct the parental imagoes in all their complexity, but it is particularly difficult to detect the preverbal contributions among all the later elaborations in the productions of the adult. Dr. Almansi sought to present criteria which might help in differentiating the earlier from the later perceptual contributions to the formation of the endopsychic image of the object. The data are centered on emotionally toned perceptual images of the parental face, hands, and voice.

First, Dr. Almansi presented material related to the myth of Medusa. Past contributions which emphasized Medusa as the frightening castrated female genital represent only one level of understanding. One constant feature in the numerous versions of the myth is the powerful eyes that turn humans into stone. The prototype of this experience in individual development is the frightened child's perception of the enraged parent's face, with attention and anxiety mainly focused on the eyes. In the analsyis of a highly ambivalent male patient, the Medusa image was visually associated with his father and other angry men. Prominent in the patient's memories of angry men was the "terrible look" in their eyes and their facial hair. The imago of this patient's father emerged in analysis as markedly split, paralleling the mixed image (lovable/terrible and male/female) of Medusa in mythology.

A detailed case history of a fourteen-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa is used to illustrate Masterson's views of the etiology, clinical manifestations, psychodynamics, and treatment of patients with the borderline syndrome. His object-relations theory stresses the importance of developmental arrest in the separation-individuation stage, with a subsequent maintenance of splitting of both self- and object representations. Effort is continually made by the borderline to avoid abandonment depression, resulting in the inability to truly perceive the self as autonomous, differentiated, complete, and separate. Masterson demonstrates through the case history the ways in which his object-relations view amplifies and expands upon Hilde Bruch's interpersonal theory in the understanding of patients with anorexia nervosa.

This report explores the ways in which personality traits of the child may contribute to disturbances in caretaker-infant interaction and lead to abuse and neglect. Forty-eight abused and/or neglected infants were observed in a structured laboratory setting. Compared with normal infants observed in the same setting, the abused/neglected infants showed a variety of distorted affective communications which interfered with mutual engagement and/or elicited negative responses in caretakers. The distortions are described under six different headings: affective withdrawal, lack of pleasure, inconsistency and unpredictability, shallowness, ambivalence/ambiguity, and negative affective communications.
