Jacob A. Arlow an Appreciation

Charles Brenner M.D.

Charles Brenner

Charles Brenner  

When plans for this Jubilee Issue were instituted, Dr. Arlow had just retired as Editor-in-Chief of the Quarterly. To all concerned, it seemed both inevitable and proper under the circumstances that the issue be dedicated to him and include a tribute that would serve to express admiration for his abilities and his accomplishments, gratitude for his devoted labors on behalf of the Quarterly as its Editor, and affection for the charming, cheerful, considerate companion of eight years of work together.

Professional journals are sometimes edited by a distinguished contributor to the literature of the field, sometimes by one whose own contributions are negligible. An argument for the first is that an authority in a field can most easily recognize excellence in others and most successfully solicit their contributions to the publication of which he or she is editor. An argument for the second is that such a one has more time and energy available for the demanding task of editing a journal than does the editor who is distracted from it by scholarly, investigative, and educational tasks apart from work on the journal itself. In fact, excellent editors can be found in both camps, as the history of the Quarterly itself attests.

Of the two, Dr. Arlow clearly belongs in the first. He is an outstanding example of a superb editor who has himself made great contributions to his chosen field. His contributions began long before he assumed his post as Editor, they continued during his term of office, and he continues to produce them with the excellence and frequency which he has accustomed us to expect from him. How Dr. Arlow is able to do so much and to do it all so well is something which constantly astonishes all who know him.

[[RunningHead]]

Joan Fleming—1904-1980

Herbert Gaskill

Herbert Gaskill

Herbert Gaskill  

Joan Fleming died August 10, 1980, ending a long and distinguished psychoanalytic career. She was a highly skilled clinician, a superb administrator, and a dedicated and tireless contributor to the scientific and educational activities of the American Psychoanalytic Association.

Dr. Fleming obtained an A.B. from Wellesley College in 1924 and a master's in physiology from Oberlin College in 1928. She taught physical education and physiology prior to entering medical school at the University of Chicago (M.D., 1936). Internship and psychiatric residency were at the University of Chicago. In 1943 she was certified in psychiatry by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology. She completed psychoanalytic training at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis (1941-1945). She was a member of the staff of the Psychiatric and Psychosomatic Institute, Michael Reese Hospital (1951-1960), as well as being affiliated with a number of other facilities in Chicago.

Dr. Fleming, a member of the faculty of the Chicago Institute for two decades, was appointed a training and supervisory analyst in 1952. As Dean of Education (1952-1969), she led and inspired the educational experiences of a continuing line of psychoanalytic candidates. Throughout her career, she also maintained an active interest in the teaching of psychoanalytic principles to those in allied mental health disciplines, particularly social workers.

In 1969 she moved to Denver to become Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Colorado School of Medicine and to join the faculty of the Denver Psychoanalytic Institute. The impact of her extensive clinical and educational experience on the development of the newly organized Institute cannot be overestimated.

On the Quest for the Origins of Conflict

Theodore Shapiro M.D.

Theodore Shapiro

Theodore Shapiro, M.D.
Cornell University Medical College
525 East 68th St.
New York, N.Y. 10021

Theodore Shapiro  

ABSTRACT

The psychoanalytic genetic point of view was developed initially to account for choice of symptom in terms of points of regression and the conflict that developed around the expression of drives formerly not opposed. Later, clinical problems gave rise to positing an earlier and earlier anlage for conflict and symptom formation. The data on direct observation of preverbal infants and rules for validation of retrospective constructs are reviewed. The psychoanalyst's interpretation of symbols is emphasized as the most cultivated skill of our science. A restraint on genetic theory formation derives from the discontinuities in method between the task of analyzing and that of infant observation.

Mark Kanzer M.D.

Mark Kanzer

Mark Kanzer, M.D.
16 Sunnyridge Road
Harrison, N.Y. 10528

Mark Kanzer  

ABSTRACT

Freud's "scientific psychology" is traced from 1888 to 1938 in the succession of mental apparatuses he proposed. The key proposition, for which he shared credit with Theodor Lipps after 1898, holds that consciousness is a sense organ for detecting and translating the unknown inner reality of the unconscious. The significance of this approach from the standpoint of the methodology, constructions, and metapsychology of psychoanalysis is considered and compared with other views of metapsychology now current.

[[RunningHead]]

The Development of Aggression in Early Childhood

By Henri Parens. New York: Jason Aronson, 1979. 399 pp.

Judith Schachter

Judith Schachter

Judith S. Schachter
PITTSBURGH

Judith Schachter  

Dr. Parens's erudite, difficult, and thought-provoking book requires careful reading, rereading, and cogitation. He attempts to delineate both the view of aggression in current Freudian metapsychology and its ontogenesis and role in the first five years of life. His ten years as principal investigator of an early childhood development program and his many years of experience as a child analyst have impressed him with the usefulness of Margaret Mahler's theory of symbiosis and separation-individuation, as a frame of reference both for child observation and for the understanding of early intrapsychic processes.

The first section of the book, a review of the psychoanalytic theory of aggression, is written in a scholarly, footnoted, and closely reasoned style. It includes a well-rounded and succinct historical recounting and formulation of Freud's theories interspersed with criticism of other theorists. Parens is a strong proponent of the pre-death-instinct formulations of aggression and critical of Hartmann's proposition that the ego is endowed with innate, non-instinctual energy. Aggression and sexuality are assumed to be on a par with each other as the two essential drives subsuming all instinctual impulses. The nondestructive trend in aggression is defined according to the 1915 criteria for instinctual drives; it is thus seen as serving and motivating the ego's task to master and to adapt as well to insure the gratification of libidinal and narcissistic wishes.

277

[[RunningHead]]

A Note on the Phallic Significance of Spitting

Herbert Gomberg M.D.

Herbert Gomberg

Herbert L. Gomberg, M.D.
8226 Douglas Ave., Suite 430
Dallas, Texas 75225

Herbert Gomberg  

That "the ejection of fluid from the mouth [may represent] an ejaculation or urination" (Lewin, 1933, p. 25) is an old observation in the analytic literature. Nevertheless, with the current emphasis on prephallic pathology, it is important not to lose sight of the continuing validity of old observations. It is not that these observations have been superseded, but we now hope to integrate them within a more complex schema. In the excitement and interest over what is current and new, however, what is known or was known in the past may be de-emphasized and, with our attention turned elsewhere, forgotten. That this process has its unconscious determinants is a point that need hardly be mentioned to any working psychoanalyst. Still, what we do not think of regularly is harder to perceive in our patients' associations. This holds as much for what was once known but now de-emphasized as for what is new or, as yet, unconceptualized.

In my experience the equation of spitting and urination-ejaculation is frequent and significant in both men and women. While in two of the three cases I will present, anal phase (soiling) elements were also prominent in this context and were interpreted, and issues of separation, identity, and narcissism were present as well, it was important that the specifically phallic significance of spitting was not ignored. In the following vignettes it is this aspect that is emphasized. I do not mean to suggest that these phallic phase determinants of spitting are the sole important aspects to be analyzed. In the second case, for example, oral rage and envy and sadomasochistic issues from all stages, oral and anal as well as phallic, were prominent throughout the analysis.

90

[[RunningHead]]

Intrapsychic and Interpersonal Dimensions of Treatment. A Clinical Dialogue

By Robert Langs, M.D. and Harold F. Searles, M.D. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1980. 323 pp.

Leon Ferber

Leon Ferber

Leon Ferber
LAUREL, FLA.

Leon Ferber  

This book is a transcription of four tape-recorded dialogues between the two authors. It ranges over many aspects of the use of psychoanalysis and psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy, with little differentiation between the two therapeutic modes. The clinical material offered predominantly concerns the treatment of schizophrenic patients, although clinically undocumented comments and claims are made about classical psychoanalysis and the analyzability of borderlines and psychotics. There are both differences and similarities in the approaches of these two men, the details of which have been elaborated upon extensively by each in their publications and presentations.

Searles offers a detailed set of revelations about himself in the discussion, "The Development of a Psychoanalyst," which seems to include no great concern over the impact that such information might have on past and future analysands and therapies. Langs indicates how his views have been influenced by and derived from those of Melanie Klein, Winnicott, Bion, Masud Khan, André Green, and certain Latin American analysts such as the Barangers, Racker, etc. Both Langs and Searles consider themselves far more willing to deal with primitive mental phenomena in themselves and in their patients than are classical analysts who do not adhere to the views and techniques they espouse.

Langs's by now well-reiterated ideas about the bipersonal field and its frame are reviewed as part of his emphasis on the adaptational interactional or interpersonal dimensions of the therapeutic situation. His view of the central position of the unconscious communication between the analyst and patient leads him to the ultimate statement that he takes everything that the patient says as a commentary, valid or distorted, about the analyst.

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. VIII, 1979

Transition or Transformation? Personal and Political Development of Former Berkeley Free Speech Movement Activists. Alberta J. Nassi and Stephen I. Abramowitz. Pp. 21-35.

Former Berkeley Free Speech Movement activists' sociopolitical status, self and ideal self constructions, perceptions of parents' child-rearing practices, and moral reasoning were compared with an assessment made eleven years earlier following the Berkeley Sproul Hall sit-in. Activists were found to be less politically active, more tempered in their political radicalism, more pragmatic and more personally reactive in their self and ideal self conceptualizations, more critical in their perceptions of parental relationships, and stable in their level of moral development. While activists appear to have made some important life transitions, an argument is made for their continued distinctiveness as a generational cohort both politically and psychosocially.

[[RunningHead]]

Theories of Pathogenesis

Jacob Arlow M.D.

Jacob Arlow

Jacob A. Arlow, M.D.
120 East 36 St.
New York, N.Y. 10016

Jacob Arlow  

ABSTRACT

Theories of pathogenesis can be influenced by shared unconscious fantasies. This may determine the speedy enthusiasm with which some theories are accepted. In keeping with primitive, pleasure-seeking trends, it is appealing to blame illness on others and to view pathogenesis in terms of the intrusion into the self of some alien, noxious agent. These ideas can be seen in certain current theories that ascribe pathogenesis to inadequate, unempathic mothering. Such theories influence psychoanalytic technique. Analysis becomes a form of replacement therapy, in which the analyst facilitates normal development by serving as an appropriate object. This approach may gratify unconscious needs in analyst and analysand alike. The attempt to isolate one specific pathogenic factor as crucial fails to do justice to the complexity of pathogenesis and may lead to the failure to recognize the role of unconscious conflict and to analyze resistances.

Vann Spruiell

Vann Spruiell, M.D.
1305 Antonine St.

Vann Spruiell  

ABSTRACT

Freud intentionally used Das Ich to refer to both the "self" and an abstract metapsychological system. In English, the separation of the terms "self" and "ego" has led to major problems. The word self, taken in its everyday sense, is necessarily ubiquitous in psychoanalysis. But its reflexive nature makes it impossible to define except as a series of fantasies. Self has no other place as a theoretical word. What the analysand calls his self the analyst calls ego, which is definable, either in the sense of what can be known about the analysand's experience, or as a nonexperiential abstraction.

Regression: Some General Considerations

Hans Loewald M.D.

Hans Loewald

Hans W. Loewald, M.D.
65 Trumbull St.
New Haven, Conn. 06510

Hans Loewald  

ABSTRACT

Regression is a concept involving developmental as well as structural considerations. Clinically speaking, it refers both to psychopathology and to potentially therapeutic phases of the psychoanalytic process. Regression, a movement backward, reverts to more or less primitive stages of psychic organization which deviate from a norm, while at the same time these stages are enduringly active in the continual integration of psychic life. Regression and progression are necessary and complementary phases of this organizing activity. Certain theoretical and clinical aspects are discussed in some detail. The normative implications of regression, in the context of modern Western rationality as the standard of normal mental life, are briefly considered.

Edward Weinshel  

ABSTRACT

In the regression from the oedipal impulses some, perhaps many, people retreat to the introjective (oral) mode of defense. This and other defensive maneuvers culminate in a variety of behaviors which have been extensively and variously described in the literature. The authors describe, under the rubric of "gaslighting," an outcome of the introjective defense in which a victim and a victimizer join psychological modes in expressing and defending themselves against oral, incorporative impulses (greed), each in his or her own way.

Some Thoughts on the "Here and Now" in Psychoanalytic Technique and Process

Leo Stone M.D.

Leo Stone

Leo Stone, M.D.
One Gracie Terrace
New York, N.Y. 10028

Leo Stone  

ABSTRACT

This paper consists of a series of reflections on the "here and now" in analysis, stimulated by recent renewed interest in the subject. The subject is considered briefly in historical perspective. In addition to the central issue of transference interpretation, a broader conception of current process is briefly examined. The entire "here and now" complex is viewed as dynamically indispensable to the effective reconstruction of the past. The critical role of the transference neurosis is stated. Certain dynamic and technical desiderata are developed. The importance of adequate attention to the patient's "reality" is emphasized in its multiple references.

[[RunningHead]]

Adaptation in Schizophrenia. The Theory of Segmental Set

David Shakow, Ph.D. New York: John Wiley & Sons, 1979. 245 pp.

Ping-Nie Pao

Ping-Nie Pao

Ping-Nie Pao
ROCKVILLE, MD.

Ping-Nie Pao  

As an experimental psychologist, Shakow devoted half a century to his research efforts on schizophrenia. This book, crystallized out of Shakow's work in his long association with the psychological laboratories at the Worcester State Hospital and the National Institute of Mental Health, "conceptualizes and analyzes the major differences between schizophrenia and normal psychological processes by delineating the stimulus/internal process/response functions (the basic operations of behavior) and the accompanying processes of perception and segmental sets" (p. 151).

On the basis of data derived from five groups of research experiments—physiological, physiopsychological, psychophysiological, experimental psychological and clinical psychological, Shakow came to the conclusion that, in terms of the stimulus/internal process/response model, a schizophrenic patient's stimulus receptive system is not at fault, but his or her responses are "out of balance in their cognitive, affective, and conative aspects, as well as in their speed, intensity, and content" (p. 151). Thus, Shakow states, "My hypothesis is that generalized set is not available to [a schizophrenic]. During schizophrenic episodes, it has been replaced by segmental set, a pathological state of set functioning" (p. 15).

Since some of the terms used in previous quotations are more familiar to experimental psychologists than to practicing psychoanalysts, it might be helpful to have these terms clarified. According to Shakow, "set" is "the mechanism nature has provided to make attending more efficient, enabling the organism to adapt more effectively to the increasing complexities of its expanding and changing environment. Set presumes the existence of structures that obviate the necessity of a new act of attending with each change in sensation or response, but nevertheless allows for continuing change" (p. 13).

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

M'Uzan adopts Neyraut's wide definition of countertransference which gives it precedence over the transference. He is concerned with a certain type of analytic phenomenon in which the analyst suddenly finds in himself strange images, unexpected phrases, abstract formulas, more or less elaborate reveries, etc. He believes that even without countertransference elements, these episodes prove singularly helpful in understanding the patient's material. He hypothesizes that at such a moment the analyst has been "invaded" by the analysand and that the analyst's psychic apparatus has become that of the analysand. He would like to call such phenomena "paradoxical thought," and the system to which such thoughts belong would be a "paradoxical system." M'Uzan prefers to explain such phenomena through a biological analogy of immunity and recognition of foreign bodies. He believes that such a paradoxical system occurs with the inhibition, on a momentary or partial basis, of the functions which permit the recognition of the other person and which protect against such merging. He links his concept with certain aspects of Greenacre's work on identity and with Lacan's mirror stage.

Psyche. XXXIII, 1979

Robert Musil—The Dilemma of a Post-Freudian Writer of the Type "Poeta Doctus." Johannes Cremerius. Pp. 733-772.

Musil's novel, The Man without Qualities, is described as a "psychoanalytic novel par excellence," and the novelist's thorough study of psychoanalysis is documented by reference to his published legacy. Before Freud conceptualized the problems of humanity within the framework of his scientific psychology of the unconscious, writers had construed these with their own homespun psychology. Since then, there seemed to remain only the alternatives of dilettantism or of manufacturing pathographies à la Freud. Musil chose the third alternative of "forgetting" his own study of Freud, that is, of concealing it in order to realize his projected description of the world in a second, post-Freudian naïveté. His novel raises the question of how one can write and live in two interrelated worlds—the scientifically demystified world and the world as we all experience it.

308

Extreme Traumatizations as Cumulative Trauma; Psychoanalytic Investigations of the Effects of Concentration Camp Experiences on Survivors and Their Children. Ilse Grubrich-Simitis. Pp. 991-1023.

Psychoanalysts, too, tend to withhold their empathy in reaction to the destruction fantasies which were realized under the Nazi regime and to the "psychotic cosmos" established in the concentration camps. This explains why the effects of extreme traumatization, which the inmates of German death camps suffered and which have become known as "survivor syndrome," have been only gradually recognized and studied. Those who escaped, having been the victims of traumas which crush any psychic structure, pass their disturbances on to their children by way of overtaxing legacies. Thus a cumulative trauma is inflicted on the second generation.

Psychoanalysis and Dynamic Psychotherapy—Similarities and Differences Twenty-Five Years Later

Leo Rangell M.D.

Leo Rangell

Leo Rangell, M.D.
456 North Carmelina Ave.
Los Angeles, Calif. 90049

Leo Rangell  

PREFACE

In the 1930's when this Quarterly was born, psychoanalysis was achieving its maturity with the addition of ego psychology to the psychology of the drives. During that decade the concern was to preserve the identity of psychoanalysis in the midst of derivative schools which emphasized mainly cultural factors at the expense of the internal psychic world. In the 1940's the success of the newly established discipline came to be widely appreciated in its applicability to emotional disturbances during World War II. In the 1950's, in the flush of its accepted status and now dominant position in Departments of Psychiatry, the task became to facilitate its growth while continuing to prevent its identity from being blurred.

This was the ambience in 1954 when a cluster of papers and panels were published delineating the similarities and differences between psychoanalysis and dynamic psychotherapy, its most important derivative technique. Published at the same time were several panels on the diagnosis and treatment of the borderline state.

In 1979 the Southern Regional Psychoanalytic Societies sponsored a symposium in Atlanta, Georgia, hosted by the Atlanta Psychoanalytic Society, at which three authors who had contributed to the 1954 discussions were invited to update their views on "Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy, Similarities and Differences, a 25-Year Perspective." The participants were Merton M. Gill, Leo Stone, and I.

Psychic Conflict and the Concept of Defense

Sander Abend M.D.

Sander Abend

Sander M. Abend, M.D.
1040 Park Ave.
New York, N.Y. 10028

Sander Abend  

ABSTRACT

Anna Freud's classic work, The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence, is reassessed from the perspective of our current understanding of its place in the history of psychoanalytic theory. The subsequent development of the concept of defense is then traced, with emphasis on its relationship to psychic conflict. The role of both defense and conflict in normal and pathological behavior is stressed.

ABSTRACT

This paper, the second in a series of four tracing the development of Freud's theory of instinctual drives, deals with the elaboration of the 1905 theory of sexuality, the introduction of ego drives contrasted with sexual drives, and the relation of drive theory to the topographic theory of the mental apparatus, as these issues were presented by Freud up to and including 1915.

ABSTRACT

This is the first of a series of four papers which trace the development of Freud's theory of instinctual drives. Extra-Analytic Contacts: Theoretical and Clinical Considerations

Herbert Strean D.S.W.

Herbert Strean

Herbert S. Strean, D.S.W.
7 West 96 St.
New York, N.Y. 10025

Herbert Strean  

ABSTRACT

The literature on the extra-analytic contact is reviewed and a case is presented in which the extra-analytic contacts of patient and analyst were analyzed. Three types of extra-analytic contacts are discussed: (1) those actively brought about by the patient; (2) those that are "accidental" for both parties; and (3) those that are anticipated by the analyst but not by the patient. The extra-analytic encounter can heighten latent transference and countertransference themes, clarify certain resistances, and serve as an index of therapeutic progress. It can also interfere with an analysis by raising false hopes for the patient and can dilute the analyst's position as a fantasied object.

[[RunningHead]]

Legend, Myth, and Magic in the Image of the Artist. A Historical Experiment

By Ernst Kris and Otto Kurz. New Haven and London: Yale University Press, 1979. 159 pp.

Eugene Glynn

Eugene Glynn

Eugene Glynn
NEW YORK

Eugene Glynn  

Ernst Kris had his beginnings as an art historian when the coal shortage in Vienna during the first World War forced his school to part-time schedules. The young boy used the mornings so freed to attend art history lectures at the Vienna University. By his late

101

twenties he had published what was to become a standard text in its highly specialized field, a field too restricting for a mind like Kris's, Renaissance gems and intaglios. It was marriage that brought him into the contact with Freud's personal circle and its intellectual world that led him to undertake psychoanalytic training. The dual training produced, in time, classic studies on art and the creative imagination; the first was a study of the psychotic Austrian baroque sculptor, Franz Xavier Messerschmidt. Here, forty-five years after its original German publication and at last in English, is the second, Die Legende vom Kunstler: Ein historischer Versuch, its title rendered more cautiously explicit. That first edition, much sought after, has long disappeared; its ideas, if not their source, have become surprisingly familiar, particularly to readers of Kris's later psychoanalytic works or the studies of the Warburg group. Indeed, the volume is dedicated to the Warburg Institute.

Kurz, eight years Kris's junior, was an intellectual prodigy to match, himself at the start of a distinguished career when the two men joined their disparate but already formidable skills on this essay. Both had been students of Julius von Schlosser, both contributing editorial services to the Viennese professor's great survey of the art historical literature. Kris was already leading an astounding double life: eight hours a day an assistant curator at the Vienna Kunsthistorische Museum, he saw his psychoanalytic patients early and late. His interest had been stirred by a discovery he had made while working on the life of Messerschmidt. In his biography, he found embedded a legend—the start in life as youthful shepherd—long and often told of other artists. Kurz, mining the art historical lode, discovered a story of Vasari's about Fra Filippo Lippi to have been taken directly from an Italian novella. Vasari's "plagiarism" turned out to be a mode of proceeding common enough in biographies of artists from antiquity on. An often determining image of the artist seemed at work in the mind of biographers, independent of artists' historical lives. The history of this myth was needed, and some speculation: what purpose did it serve?—the question perhaps the most basic of psychoanalytic inquiries. Here the men were cautious, for their intellectual commitments differed. The methodology was to be "strictly historical," psychological interpretation referred to only "summarily and in passing.

[[RunningHead]]

The Adolescent Passage. Developmental Issues

By Peter Blos. New York: International Universities Press, Inc., 1979. 521 pp.

Austin Silber

Austin Silber

Austin Silber
NEW YORK

Austin Silber  

This collection of papers, all but the last previously published, summarizes the author's contributions to the study of adolescence, in which a developmental point of view has been productive of many instructive observations and conceptualizations. Written clearly and well, the formulations are supported by ample clinical data and are

110

buttressed by a scholarly mastery of the relevant analytic literature. The book succeeds in its aim to enable the clinician better to distinguish pathology from those aspects of adolescent behavior and emotional states which are normal for the adolescent process. It is rich in information about a period of life which must be understood in the analysis of every adult patient.

The titles of the sections of the book under which the papers are grouped give a view of the scope and the emphases of this volume. Under the heading, "The Mutual Influence of the Adolescent and His Surround," the importance of successfully negotiating each phase of development as a requirement for effectively dealing with the developmental demands of the next phase of life is highlighted with impressive clinical detail. Blos notes that some middle-class latency youngsters coming from progressive and liberal backgrounds may be so overburdened by close family ties, so steeped in accepting and understanding attitudes, that it is most difficult for them to modify and alter libidinal attachments. Such an upbringing, during which object relations are not replaced by identifications, can interfere with normal latency development. The ego's successful negotiation of latency is a necessary prerequisite for healthy adolescent development. Those youngsters in whom latency ties are not loosened are frequently unprepared to deal with the normal adolescent regression, which is then experienced as a developmental obstacle rather than as an adaptive and progressive element in their growing up.

The task of the adolescent ego is to bring to bear, through the mandatory developmental regression, the resolution of the infantile conflicts which the enfeebled ego of the preoedipal years was unable to resolve. Blos is never quite clear, however, whether this restructuring is dependent on therapeutic intervention with necessary interpretation or whether it occurs automatically in a healthy adolescent. One almost gets the impression that this obligatory regression can itself be therapeutic. From the case material it seems more likely that the evolving understanding which helps the adolescent define what is infantile and conflict laden in his preoedipal years helps bring about the necessary psychic restructuring.

Adolescent Psychiatry. VI, 1978

The Diagnosis of Borderline Conditions in Adolescence. Otto F. Kernberg. Pp. 298-319.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

The carefully worked out structural diagnostic criteria differentiating the borderline conditions from neuroses and psychoses are reviewed: i.e., the presence of identity diffusion, the predominance of primitive defensive operations, particularly splitting, and the maintenance of reality testing. We are reminded of the particular difficulties in applying these criteria to adolescents whose tendency to engage in identity crises, to show striking superficial psychopathology, and to display multiple transient sexual trends may mask diagnoses of all kinds. These difficulties are beautifully clarified in six illustrative case histories. Kernberg reviews his distinction between "narcissistic personality" and "borderline personality organization," emphasizing that only the most severe narcissistic personalities present with overt borderline functioning. In the treatment of the borderline adolescent, Kernberg emphasizes the need for absence of either "moralistic" or "romanticizing" attitudes toward the patient, as well as the need to set firm criteria with both patient and family about the conditions for treatment. though recognizing the need at times for family evaluation and possible family treatment, he advises great caution against confusion of goals with this approach.

Adolescent Psychiatry. VI, 1978

Separation-Individuation of an Identical Twin. Elisabeth Lassers and Robert Nordan. Pp. 469-479.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

The authors present a fascinating case history of the successful resolution, in therapy, of separation-individuation problems in a bright identical twin woman in her early to mid-twenties. The case confirms the authors' hypothesis that twinning can interfere with the normal process of separation-individuation in the following pattern: 1) mothers may be forced to offer less than optimal need-fulfillment because of the added burdens of having two babies at once; 2) twins, frustrated by unmet needs, may turn to one another for solace, thus enhancing the development of symbiosis rather than separation; and 3) the private communications developed particularly by identical twins may alienate the mother and reinforce the symbiosis. This symbiosis may remain lifelong or may end in a delayed working through of separation-individuation in late adolescence or early adulthood.

The Tragic Effect. The Oedipus Complex in Tragedy

By André Green. Translated by Alan Sheridan. Cambridge/London/New York: Cambridge University Press, 1979. 264 pp.

Leonard Shengold

Leonard Shengold

Leonard Shengold
NEW YORK

Leonard Shengold  

The French title of this book—Un oeil de trop (An Eye Too Many), part of a quotation from Hölderlin about Oedipus—is happier than the English one. For it is the power of the "extra eye" that is central to this brilliant work. The phrase alludes to a power of the mind that, to quote Flaubert's definition of the true artist, belongs to the "triple thinker." André Green knows that psychoanalysts need the "third eye" as well as the "third ear" to do their clinical work. The ability to turn this mental force, which is capable of operating in and with multiple dimensions—of performing in contrapuntal perception—to the extraclinical has not been granted to many psychoanalysts. Our first and greatest mind—Freud—valued, made use of, and contributed understanding to the complexity and mysterious creative power of myth and literature; but often psychoanalytic critics of art and artists (and sometimes Freud himself) have proceeded with a crudely reductionist hermeneutical bent. We are fortunate that André Green is able to be a "triple thinker" who has not only the necessary erudition, but a subtle, critical intelligence capable of containing contradictions and maintaining ambiguities—an intelligence that respects but is not paralyzed by the mysteries of artistic creativity and of the mind.

Green presents the theater as a metaphor for the mind. He elaborates on Freud's quotation from Fechner about dreams taking place on a "scene of action" (Schauplatz—literally showplace) different from that of waking ideational life.1 Freud called Fechner's remark, in a letter to Fliess dated February 9, 1898, the "only sensible" one in the literature on dreams.2

1Freud, S. (1916-1917). Introductory lectures on psycho-analysis. S.E., 15: p. 90.2Freud, S. (1887-1902). The Origins of Psycho-Analysis. Letters to Wilhelm Fliess, Drafts and Notes. New York: Basic Books, 1954, pp. 244-245.286

The Reproduction of Mothering. Psychoanalysis and the Sociology of Gender

By Nancy Chodorow. Berkeley/Los Angeles/London: University of California Press, 1978. 263 pp.

Miriam Wimpfheimer and Bonnie Kaufman

Bonnie Kaufman

Miriam J. Wimpfheimer
NEW YORK
Bonnie Kaufman
NEW YORK

Bonnie Kaufman  

In The Reproduction of Mothering Nancy Chodorow presents a theory based on sociological and psychoanalytic ideas of how the psychological identity and social role of mothering gets passed on from mother to daughter through the generations. She examines the effects of this mothering tradition on the identities of men and women, on family structure, sexual relations, ideology about women, and on society at large. Rejecting arguments based on biology and cognitive-social role learning, Chodorow claims that women's psychological mothering is a feature of social structure and therefore requires an explanation in terms of social structure. Her methodology combines the psychoanalytic sociology of Parsons and the Frankfurt School with psychoanalytic object-relations theory. The argument favors primary parenting by men as well as by women, leading to freedom from rigid sexual identities and roles, a change that would give women a share of the power in society and men a chance to further develop their emotional capacities. Chodorow's ideas, though biased, are clever and broad-ranging, pointing to deep and subtle connections between personality and the outer world of the family and social structure. She invites those in the psychoanalytic field to focus on the "sociological and structural foundations of what they observe clinically."

In her basic argument Chodorow uses the word "mothering" with its psychological (primary emotional tie with infant, nurturer, supporter, socializer)

[[RunningHead]]

Aggression in the Service of Separation-Individuation—Case Study of a Mother-Daughter Relationship

Margaret Mahler M.D.

Margaret Mahler

Margaret S. Mahler, M.D.
10 West 66 St.
New York, N.Y. 10023

Margaret Mahler  

Recent work has contributed to a better understanding of the use of aggression in personality development, without, however, dispelling the pejorative connotation which the term aggression has acquired in the course of the decades since Freud's double drive theory came into existence.

In recent years, the difficulties of resolving mother-daughter conflicts in the preoedipal, oedipal, and postoedipal realm have occupied a rather large segment of psychoanalytic literature.

The following account of such a mother-daughter relationship, derived from longitudinal observation and supported by reconstruction with psychoanalytically oriented interviews, yielded interesting data on how aggression was used in the service of disengagement and distancing for successful separation-individuation at first, and how it was utilized for the maintenance of individual identity later on.

In the beginning of life, libido and aggression, indistinguishable from each other, are part of the undifferentiated matrix. Later, they form a kind of chemical alloy from which the isolation, the teasing out, of the aggressive elements is most often impossible. Aggression always contains an admixture of libido, and libidinal phases always contain an admixture of aggression.

Even if we avoid the issue of whether aggression is or is not a primary instinctual drive, the question of the source of aggression still comes up.

Typical Examination Dreams, "Superego Dreams," and Traumatic Dreams

Owen Renik M.D.

Owen Renik

Owen Renik, M.D.
2300 Sutter St., Suite 201
San Francisco, Calif. 94115

Owen Renik  

ABSTRACT

Typical examination dreams fulfill, in disguised form, a wish to be reassured about the future. Similar disguised wish fulfillments can be identified in certain "superego dreams" and in those post-traumatic dreams in which a traumatic event is accurately re-enacted. Recognition of the wish and the need for disguise permits a fuller picture of the dreamer's immediate conflicts to emerge. Vignettes are presented to illustrate the implications for clinical work. The concepts of the repetition compulsion and a motivation toward mastery in dreaming are considered in light of these observations.

responseSet.title: From the Literature on Neonatology
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

From the Literature on Neonatology

Scott Dowling M.D.

Scott Dowling

Scott Dowling  

It is no longer news that William James was wrong; the neonate is not "a buzzing, blooming confusion." Neither is it true that early infancy is a time of walled-off autistic functioning with only occasional forays into contact with the environment. Beginning with Peter Wolff's (1959), (1966) discoveries regarding infant states and their relationship to infant functioning, each passing year has extended our knowledge of infant capacities and their adaptive significance. The neonate (birth to two months) is now known to be an organized and organizing being, not only responsive to inner rhythms and needs, but also initiating and participating in a perceptual and motoric dialogue with the outer world of things and people. This is not to suggest that we have found infants to be "mature" or that they possess a form of psychological organization which would be familiar to us from child or adult functioning. At best, we know only the lineaments of that organization, but what we know is sufficient to say confidently that its qualitative richness and adaptive value, especially in eliciting attachment responses, far exceeds the presumptions of past theories. In this commentary I will discuss two of the more recent findings which confound traditional views of the infant; they are the related demonstrations of neonatal "imitation" and intermodal matching.

In 1953, René Zazzo, Director of the Laboratory of Infant Psychobiology, Institute des Hautes Études, Paris, stated:

The origins of imitation are still rather mysterious. Eight years ago I observed a fact which I consider almost inexplicable. I noticed in my son, who was then twenty days old, the imitation of putting out the tongue. At first I thought it was a mistake, that it was I who had imitated the child and not the child who had imitated me. I tried this experiment again several times. I took a film of it and later I was able to examine six infants in whom this imitation also appeared between the twentieth and thirtieth day, then disappeared, and reappeared at the age of about three months (Tanner and Inhelder, 1956, p. 72).

Character Traits and Object Relationships

Joseph Sandler Ph.D.

Joseph Sandler

Joseph Sandler, Ph.D.
Simund Freud Center The Hebrew University
Jerusalem, Israel 91905

Joseph Sandler  

ABSTRACT

Character traits have in the past been viewed as "discharge" phenomena and compromise formations. Many traits can be better understood, however, as devices for evoking particular types of response in others in order to actualize the wished-for relationships existing in unconscious fantasy. Moreover, some "evocative" character traits create the unconscious illusion of the presence of the love objects. The concept of unconscious illusion can also be used to clarify the notion of "introject," which may be understood as an illusory object perceived outside normal consciousness.

Mirror Lake Drive
Lake Placid, N.Y. 12946

David Beres  

ABSTRACT

"Self" as an isolated term is an abstraction. The concept of self, on the other hand, is an important component of psychoanalytic psychology. Does the designation of "self" as a superordinate agency add to our understanding? This paper considers the relation of the concept of self to the structural theory. In both theory and clinical practice the concept of self is prominently associated with the concepts of identity and narcissism. The latter are discussed briefly. Illustrative cases are included.

A Note on Narcissism

W. Meissner S.J.

W. Meissner

W. W. Meissner, S.J.
6 Sumner Rd.
Cambridge, Mass. 02138

W. Meissner  

ABSTRACT

The connection of the concept of narcissism with the concept of the self is re-examined in the light of Hartmann's formulation of narcissism as cathexis of the self. While the formula is valid, its converse remains open to question. Implications for a psychology of the self independent of (but not divorced from) the dynamics of narcissism are suggested in regard to the understanding of perversions, development, narcissistic object relations, and self-esteem. The viability of a separate psychology of the self in each area is proposed.

[[RunningHead]]

The Selected Papers of Margaret S. Mahler, M.D.

Vol. I: Infantile Psychosis and Early Contributions; Vol. II: Separation-Individuation. New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1979. 306 pp., 263 pp.

Robert Tyson

Robert Tyson

Robert L. Tyson
LA JOLLA, CA.

Robert Tyson  

An excellent introduction to Mahler's Selected Papers is provided by Marjorie Harley and Annemarie P. Weil, themselves notable contributors to the psychoanalytic literature. They concisely trace the major themes evident in Mahler's published work (of which these

107

two volumes are but a selection) beginning in 1942, and they provide a perspective useful both to the student new to Mahler's thinking and to those already familiar with it.

With an increasing focus on the second year of life, Mahler's interests grew to encompass the motifs of motility, the role of affect in mother-infant communication and development, the developmental history of omnipotence, and comparisons between usual developmental variations and pathological phenomena. The culminating conceptualization of the separation-individuation subphases seems now a natural and inevitable consequence of this work published between 1942 and 1976, based primarily on clinical experience, and gathered in Volume I. Significant contributions along the way include, among others, the distinction between autistic and symbiotic psychoses, the recognition of the importance of the child's innate endowment and the fact that a psychotic infant may evoke deviant and deleterious responses from an otherwise "good enough" mother, and the clarification of the importance of the father in the preoedipal period. Not all of these contributions have been pursued and exploited. As another example of observation which awaits further investigation and refinement, consider the following: while the mother may be less involved in the care of her infant than a nurse who provides immediate need satisfaction, the mother's image seems to attract so much more investment "that it often, though not always, becomes the cardinal object representation" (Vol. I, "On Sadness and Grief in Infancy and Childhood: Loss and Restoration of the Symbiotic Love Object," 1961, p. 263). We still find it easier to explain why certain mothers "fail" than to explain why other mothers "succeed" with their infants.

[[RunningHead]]

Sexual Excitement. Dynamics of Erotic Life

By Robert J. Stoller, M.D. New York: Pantheon Books, 1979. 281 pp.

Daniel Jaffe

Daniel Jaffe

Daniel S. Jaffe
WASHINGTON, D.C.

Daniel Jaffe  

The author's previous works on gender identity and on the dynamics of perversions have led him to his present effort to formulate a theory of sexual excitement. Following his earlier ideas, he believes that the mental factors present in perversions contribute to sexual excitement in general, since there is a continuum from normal to perverse.

His theory, briefly stated, is that it is hostility, the desire to harm another person, that generates sexual excitement. The hostility is seen as an attempt to undo the childhood traumata and frustration that threatened the development of one's masculinity or femininity via castration anxiety. The factors that perversions and sexual excitement have in common, then, are hostility, mystery, risk, illusion, revenge, reversal of trauma (or frustration) to achieve triumph, safety, and dehumanization (fetishization). Excitement operates as a dialectic between the positive and negative outcome regarding pleasure/pain or danger/safety.

The corollary of this hypothesis is stated: it is only in the rare people who can contain sexual excitement and love within the same relationship that hostility and secrecy play an insignificant part.

[[RunningHead]]

The Birth of the Living God. A Psychoanalytic Study

By AnaMaria Rizzuto, M.D. Chicago: The University of Chicago Press, 1979. 246 pp.

Howard Stein

Howard Stein

Howard F. Stein
OKLAHOMA CITY

Howard Stein  

This work is a loving, discursive, theoretical, and clinical essay on the psychogenesis of belief in God, or, in Rizzuto's terms, "God representation." Twice, at the beginning of the Introduction and at the Conclusion, she insists that "This is not a book on religion." "It is a book on object relations … about one object relation: that of man with that special object he calls God. God, psychologically speaking, is an illusory transitional object" (p. 177), one which, rather than being gradually decathected, is increasingly cathected. She identifies religion as being primarily a private, and secondarily a social, phenomenon. "The birth of the living God" consists of the early formation and lifelong modification of the God-representation (p. 41).

The first third of the book is a masterful review of the psychoanalytic literature on religion, from Freud through object-relations theory and on to the author's beloved Winnicott. Central to her argument is Winnicott's theory of transitional phenomena, the intermediate area of illusion and play which must not be questioned. The transitional object is found, yet created; similarly, God is both found and created at each new level of developmental integration. Unlike all other objects, however, "He is the only relevant object who had not undergone and cannot undergo reality testing… The believer, in spite of the uncommon nature of the relation, is not psychotic, or even necessarily neurotic. He or she may be an emotionally mature person" (p. 49). The middle chapters, case studies, richly portray four patients and the roles which God representations play in their dynamics, ranging from protective to persecutory to absent to enigmatic.

Throughout, Rizzuto seeks to refute the classical Freudian equation of religion with repetition compulsion, with its explicit overtones of pathology. She replaces it with an Eriksonian-epigenetic theory of religion in which, "once created, our God, dormant or active, remains a potentially available representation for the continuous process of psychic integration" (p. 180).

Attachment Theory and Its Therapeutic Implications. John Bowlby. Pp. 5-33.

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman

Marianne Makman  

This is a clear restatement of Bowlby's views about the origins and vicissitudes of human attachment behavior. In the first section he defines his theory, differentiating it from the classical psychoanalytic view of drive reduction

139

as the motivating force of human bond formation. Citing animal behavior studies as well as human, he postulates that bonds to a mothering figure develop independent of the drive for nourishment. Attachment behavior is "a class of behavior distinct from feeding and sexual behavior and of at least an equal significance in human life." The complementary caregiving role of parental figures allows the development of healthy attachment bonds. The parents must provide a secure base, encourage exploration from this base, and "intervene judiciously" when protection is needed. Application of this theory to psychopathology and psychotherapy is discussed.

140

Essay on Fetishism. Béla Grunberger. Pp. 235-254.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Grunberger is critical of current theories on fetishism which emphasize castration anxiety and the defense mechanisms of denial and splitting. The fetish is an anal part-object imprisoned in the sphincter and narcissistically invested rather than sexualized. The fetishist expresses and represents an internal conflict concerning narcissism and anality by projecting this conflict onto an external material object. Several case histories clarify this view. In the early history of the fetishist it seems that there regularly occurs a severe oral conflict which is rapidly shifted to the anal level. The fetishist's history of a profound conflict with the mother leads to a maternal imago of magical narcissistic omnipotence, as well as to that of the anal-sadistic mother upon whom the fetishist projects his own anality and sadism. There is, further, an absence or failure of the father, or a sadistic paternal figure. All these elements are to be found in the symbolic meaning of the fetish.

Cahn believes that language acquisition presupposes the acquisition of stable object relations. He believes that the lack, failure, or insufficiency of object relations can gravely compromise the linguistic function. He gives a clinical example and then discusses certain essential elements in language acquisition, together with their theoretical and technical implications. In the illustration the complex process by which the child mastered the problem of absence is delineated. In therapeutic play with the therapist, the patient was enabled to accept separation, to benefit from it, and to grow.

Attachment and Loss, Vol. III. Loss. Sadness and Depression

By John Bowlby. New York: Basic Books, 1980. 472 pp.

Isidor Bernstein

Isidor Bernstein

Isidor Bernstein
GREAT NECK, N.Y.

Isidor Bernstein  

In 1952, John Bowlby read a now classic paper at a meeting of the British Psycho-Analytical Society. The paper, entitled "A Two-Year-Old

1Volume I was reviewed in this Quarterly, 1971, 40:504-506; Volume II was reviewed in 1976, 45:307-309.418

Goes to Hospital," reported and discussed the filming by James Robertson of a child's reaction to separation. The written observations and the film were part of a research project on separation being conducted at the Tavistock Clinic. Their studies could be considered a continuation and extension of Spitz's observation of hospitalized infants separated from their mothers. Bowlby subsequently published a number of reports dealing with the formation of the child's attachment to his mother and the effects of the disruption of the bond due to separation from or loss of the mother. The culmination of his work is contained in a trilogy entitled Attachment and Loss. Volume I dealt with attachment, Volume II with separation,1 and this third and final volume is about loss.

Early in his writings, Bowlby called attention to what he saw as similarities in the responses of children and those of adults to bereavement, and this led him to the conclusion that the underlying psychological processes in both cases are the same. It is this assumption that has brought him into sharp disagreement with those whom he calls "traditional analysts," e.g., Helene Deutsch, Anna Freud, Max Schur, M. Wolfenstein, and H. Nagera. Bowlby takes exception to the restrictive usage of the term "mourning" which he claims that his critics have based on Freud's statement limiting it to those processes related to detachment from a dead person. For Bowlby, "the term 'mourning', with suitable qualifying adjectives, is used to denote a fairly wide array of psychological processes set in train by the loss of a loved person irrespective of their outcome" (p. 17). Bowlby finds himself in agreement with E. and R. Furman and with G. Kliman when he claims that young children (before adolescence) can mourn a lost parent in as "healthy" a way as an adult. Some confusion is apparent in this position, since the controversy is more over whether the reactions of young children can be considered equivalent to the mourning of adults. Nagera has reviewed in much clearer fashion the position of various authors regarding age, kinds of reactions, and application of the term "mourning" to responses of children to bereavement.2

[[RunningHead]]

The Dream in Clinical Practice

Edited by Joseph M. Natterson, M.D., New York: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1980. 498 pp.

Frank Berchenko

Frank Berchenko

Frank Berchenko
NEW YORK

Frank Berchenko  

This volume of twenty-eight essays by different authors, dealing with the clinical theory of dreams and the dream in various psychopathological states, in special therapeutic situations, and in various psychotherapeutic modalities, reaffirms the dream as the royal road to the unconscious.

The format of most of the chapters consists of a theoretical discussion of a specific subject combined with one or more relevant clinical vignettes with dreams. The volume as a whole contains a great number of illustrative dreams in their clinical settings. From these, it is apparent that many of the contributors rely on the manifest content of the dream alone for an understanding of the ongoing dynamics of the therapeutic situation and for guidance in their therapeutic interventions. In group psychotherapy the members readily interpret each others' as well as their own dreams. Roy M. Whitman in his chapter, "The Dream in Sexual Dysfunction Therapy," states that he requires the couples he treats to bring at least one dream each to every session. He believes that useful inferences are made from the manifest content of the dreams by the therapist, by the dreamer, and even by the dreamer's spouse. Frank M. Kline, in his chapter, "The Dream in the Treatment of the Disadvantaged," asserts that dreams are especially useful in clinics with multinational and multicultural populations since they transcend cultural barriers as a universal language. In training situations they are helpful to the supervisor because they are a direct communication from the patient.

Changes in the quality and manifest content of the dream help the therapist grasp the vicissitudes of a case in treatment. In the "bridging" therapeutic approach to schizophrenia, John S. Kafka observes that the more vivid and realistic the dream appears, the closer is the individual to a psychotic regression, while the more dreamlike the dreams are, the more removed is the patient from a psychotic organization. In suicidal patients a change in the manifest dream from violent scenes of death, destruction, and entrapment to more peaceful scenes, such as one of leave-taking, may often signal the final decision to commit suicide.

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot M.D.

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot, M.D.
Haringvlietstraat 39
1078 KA Amsterdam,
Holland

Jeanne Lampl-De Groot  

ABSTRACT

The similarity of the concepts, splitting and "multiple personality," has been generally overlooked. Both are originally present in all human beings, both have pathological connotations in clinical usage, but both may actually be observed in a wide variety of "normal" psychological phenomena. Some residues of each developmental phase are preserved in the depth of the mind. These remnants are the constituents of the multiple personality of human beings.

The Forbidden Quest and the Analytic Ideal: The Superego and Insight

Harold Blum M.D.

Harold Blum

Harold P. Blum, M.D.
23 The Hemlocks
Roslyn Estates, N.Y. 11576

Harold Blum  

ABSTRACT

As is evident in the history of civilization, in myths and dreams, and in Freud's self-analysis, insight has been both prohibited and heroically sought. Psychoanalytic insight into unconscious processes and contents involves a gradual transformation of inner interdictions and ideals through the tolerance of previously forbidden curiosity and knowledge. The analytic process depends upon relaxation of censorship and analysis of the motives and modes of self-criticism and self-punishment. While the superego may also uphold truth, the ideal of insight into psychic reality is relatively rare. The formation and consolidation of an analytic ideal of insight is an outgrowth of and contribution to analysis and analytic education. Analytic education should result in freedom from inner constraints on insight, in independent thought and judgment, and in a continuing "after-education."

The Role of Unconscious Homosexuality in the Paranoid Constellation

John Frosch M.D.

John Frosch

John Frosch, M.D.
Department of Psychiatry Brookdale Hospital Medical Center Linden Boulevard at Brookdale Plaza
Brooklyn, N.Y. 11212

John Frosch  

ABSTRACT

The literature dealing with Freud's original concept of unconscious homosexuality in the paranoid constellation is reviewed. Many of the more recent contributions view unconscious homosexual features as secondary to others; as such, they are pseudophenomena. This communication suggests that unconscious homosexuality in the male is denied, rejected, and projected because the passive, anal, sadomasochistic aspects are felt as degrading and humiliating. In the female, unconscious homosexuality is also felt as degrading and humiliating. In both sexes, the feeling of humiliation derives from real experiences in childhood. Unconscious homosexuality is viewed as the organizing principle in the paranoid constellation.
